Compare predictions with simulated genetic values
Use the simulated animal genetic values, excluding fixed effects and residual noise. Match by ID because pedigree, records and truth can differ in row order. This is a descriptive comparison, not an exact pedigree-covariance recovery experiment; see Scope below.
truth <- single_view$truth$latent_animal_values
at <- match(breeding_values$id, rownames(truth))
stopifnot(!anyNA(at), !anyDuplicated(rownames(truth)), ncol(truth) == 1L)
breeding_values$simulated <- as.numeric(truth[at, 1L])
record_truth <- breeding_values$simulated[match(single_view$records$animal,
  breeding_values$id)]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(record_truth,
  unname(single_view$truth$genetic_record_values), tolerance = 1e-10)))

plot_breeding_values <- function() {
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  limits <- range(breeding_values[c("simulated", "predicted")])
  for (observed in c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
    values <- breeding_values[breeding_values$observed == observed, ]
    r <- cor(values$simulated, values$predicted)
    plot(values$simulated, values$predicted, pch = 16, cex = 0.45,
      col = "#276b9260", xlim = limits, ylim = limits, asp = 1,
      xlab = "Simulated genetic value", ylab = "Predicted breeding value",
      main = sprintf("%s\nn = %d; correlation = %.3f",
        if (observed) "With observations" else "Without observations",
        nrow(values), r))
    abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "#a34427")
  }
}
plot_breeding_values()



Predicted versus simulated genetic values for all 10,000 animals, split by observation availability. The dashed line denotes equality.


The correlation describes agreement with simulated genetic values across a group; it is not an individual animal’s reliability. Predictions are shrunk toward the population mean, especially when information is limited, so equality with the simulated value is not expected for each animal. An animal without informative observations connected through the pedigree can have a zero prediction. That does not mean its actual genetic value is zero.


Inspect two simple diagnostic plots
plot_single_diagnostics <- function() {
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  qqnorm(record_results$residual, pch = 16, cex = 0.45, col = "#276b9260",
    main = "Conditional residuals", ylab = "Residual quantiles")
  qqline(record_results$residual, col = "#a34427", lwd = 2)
  boxplot(predicted ~ observed, data = breeding_values,
    names = c("Without observations", "With observations"),
    col = c("#bbccdc", "#679abb"), xlab = "", ylab = "Predicted breeding value",
    main = "Prediction distributions")
}
plot_single_diagnostics()



Conditional residual Q–Q plot and breeding-value distributions from the default single-trait fit.


The Q–Q plot helps identify unusual tails or outliers. Conditional residuals are affected by fitted animal effects, so this is an exploratory check. The boxplots show prediction spread, not prediction-error variance. Neither plot establishes predictive performance on new observations.


Save the results
A small report can combine the fit summary, parameter table, fixed-effect estimates and plots. Export labelled tables for use outside R:
results_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "gsuite-single-trait")
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(single_fit, file.path(results_dir, "fit.rds"))
write.csv(parameter_table, file.path(results_dir, "parameters.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(fixed_effects, file.path(results_dir, "fixed-effects.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(breeding_values, file.path(results_dir, "breeding-values.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
results_dir
Choose a permanent results_dir to retain these files beyond this R session. The displayed results and figures use the default seeds, gsuite 0.42.0 and gsim 0.9.0. They are a recorded example, not live output from your local run.
fitted() and residuals() follow fit$record_mapping: observed data rows, grouped by trait for multitrait fits, with missing responses excluded. Further solver and likelihood diagnostics are in diagnostics(single_fit)$native.

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
section: The same model with explicit components
text:
The same model with explicit components
The explicit form separates the formula from the covariance model. variable binds a component to a formula grouping column, traits declares its covariance coordinates, and kernel supplies relationships among animal levels. Component names such as animal are your labels. Both forms below use the same adapter and initializers as the short form above.
PED <- gs_pedigree(pedigree, id = "id", sire = "sire", dam = "dam")
vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc(variable = "id", traits = "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc(variable = "residual", traits = "BW")
)
single_explicit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data, vc = vcs, task = "reml", control = fit_control
)
head(gs_ranef(single_explicit)$animal)
To provide starting values, use vc = c(id = 1, residual = 1) in the short form, or start = 1 in each explicit descriptor. Supplied values override the automatic starts. Explicit descriptors can omit starts independently.
For a fixed-covariance solve, both covariance values must be provided and will remain fixed. This is a separate analysis, not a substitute for a failed REML fit:
single_solve <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data, pedigree = pedigree,
  vc = c(id = 1, residual = 1), task = "solve", control = fit_control
)
summary(single_solve)

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
section: Two traits: keep one row per observation unit
text:
Two traits: keep one row per observation unit
The user data frame has response columns BW and GL. Here we reshape gsim’s long records into that wide format. Missing responses stay NA: a missing GL does not discard an observed BW. Covariates and IDs for an observed response must be present and valid. For repeated observations, each row represents a separate observation unit; its paired traits share residual covariance.
multi_view <- gsim_pedigree_records(simulation, model = "multitrait",
  residual_groups = 1L, seed = 202)
long <- example_data(multi_view)
data_multi <- unique(long[c("observation_unit", "id", "sex", "cohort", "herd")])
for (trait in c("trait1", "trait2")) {
  observed <- long[long$trait == trait, ]
  response <- if (trait == "trait1") "BW" else "GL"
  data_multi[[response]] <- observed$value[
    match(data_multi$observation_unit, observed$observation_unit)]
}
head(data_multi)

multi_formulas <- list(
  BW = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  GL = GL ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id)
)
multi_fit <- gfit(
  formula = multi_formulas,
  data = data_multi, pedigree = pedigree, task = "reml", control = fit_control
)
summary(multi_fit)
head(gs_ranef(multi_fit)$id)
diagnostics(multi_fit)$converged
The animal component is a trait covariance matrix G multiplied by pedigree relationships; the residual component is a trait covariance matrix R within observation units. Each trait has its own fixed effects. Automatic G and R starts are diagonal, splitting each trait’s fixed-effect residual variance equally; zero initial correlations do not constrain estimated correlations.
In the recorded run, the genetic variances for BW and GL were 1.02397 and 0.74453, with covariance 0.41652. Their genetic correlation is \(0.41652 / \sqrt{1.02397 \times 0.74453} = 0.47704\). This describes the association between the two genetic effects, not the correlation between observed phenotypes. Residual variances were 0.58931 and 0.37586, with covariance 0.15879 within observation units. Use summary(multi_fit)$covariance to inspect these matrices and cov2cor(summary(multi_fit)$covariance$id) to obtain genetic correlations. The prediction table has one row per pedigree animal and one column per trait. Check both diagnostics(multi_fit)$status$ok and convergence before interpreting these estimates; point estimates alone do not quantify uncertainty.
For explicit components use the same descriptors, now with both trait names:
multi_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", traits = c("BW", "GL"), kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc("residual", traits = c("BW", "GL"))
)
multi_explicit <- gfit(formula = multi_formulas, data = data_multi,
  vc = multi_vcs, task = "reml", control = fit_control)
To supply G and R, use vc = list(id = G, residual = R) or start = G and start = R on the explicit components. Matrices must be positive definite; named rows and columns must match c("BW", "GL") in that order. With task = "solve", both matrices are required and remain fixed.

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
text:
Longitudinal data: genetic random regression
Keep one row per measurement, with repeated IDs. In this example genetic effects vary over time through an intercept and a linear basis time_basis = 2 * time - 1, matching the existing simulation example. The fixed time trend is included explicitly in the fixed part of the formula.
longitudinal_view <- gsim_pedigree_records(simulation, model = "longitudinal",
  random_regression_rank = 2L, residual_groups = 1L,
  minimum_records = 2L, maximum_records = 4L, seed = 203)
data_long <- example_data(longitudinal_view)
data_long$BW <- data_long$value
data_long$time_basis <- 2 * data_long$time - 1
data_long <- data_long[c("id", "BW", "sex", "cohort", "herd", "time", "time_basis")]
head(data_long)

long_formula <- BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + time_basis + (1 + time_basis | id)
long_fit <- gfit(formula = long_formula, data = data_long,
  pedigree = pedigree, task = "reml", control = fit_control)
summary(long_fit)
head(gs_ranef(long_fit)$id)
diagnostics(long_fit)$converged

long_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", traits = "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc("residual", traits = "BW")
)
long_explicit <- gfit(formula = long_formula, data = data_long,
  vc = long_vcs, task = "reml", control = fit_control)
Here the animal covariance Q is indexed by basis coefficients c("(Intercept)", "time_basis"), not by two traits. The automatic start uses a diagonal Q scaled to the basis magnitude and a positive residual variance, reusing gs_longitudinal_pedigree_start(). Predictions from gs_ranef() are the genetic intercept and slope coefficients for each animal; the genetic value at a specified time is intercept + slope × \((2t-1)\). The time column is retained as metadata when present; the model itself is defined by the basis in the formula.
The recorded run estimated genetic intercept variance 0.99357, slope variance 0.52636, intercept–slope covariance 0.34132 and residual variance 0.40618. Inspect these with summary(long_fit)$covariance. Because the basis is \(2t-1\), the intercept is the genetic value at \(t=0.5\); the slope multiplies this scaled basis, rather than time itself. Genetic variance therefore changes with time as \(Q_{11}+2(2t-1)Q_{12}+(2t-1)^2Q_{22}\) for a pedigree diagonal of one. There is no single genetic variance that describes the whole trajectory. Check fit status and convergence before using the predicted coefficients.
For supplied values, use vc = list(id = Q, residual = 1) or start = Q on the animal descriptor. Name Q’s rows and columns with the basis names above. Both values are required for task = "solve".
This example has one genetic random-regression effect and homogeneous, independent residual errors. It does not include a permanent environmental effect or a residual time-correlation model. These require additional model structure and cannot be inferred from repeated IDs alone.

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
text:
Repeatability: animal and permanent environment
The next question is how much repeatable variation is genetic and how much is due to an animal’s permanent environment. The formula contains two random intercepts. Their covariance descriptors distinguish pedigree relationships from independent permanent-environment effects.
Reuse the repeated-record IDs and covariates generated above. For this example, generate BW from the simulated animal genetic value, one permanent-environment value per observed animal, and independent record noise. Seed 204 makes this extra simulation reproducible. The same caveat about the pedigree genetic draw applies here; this is a workflow example, not a covariance-recovery experiment.
repeat_data <- data_long[c("id", "sex", "cohort", "herd")]
repeat_data$pe <- repeat_data$id
set.seed(204)
observed_ids <- unique(repeat_data$id)
permanent <- setNames(rnorm(length(observed_ids), sd = sqrt(0.4)), observed_ids)
genetic <- single_view$truth$latent_animal_values
repeat_data$BW <- 2 + 0.2 * (repeat_data$sex == "M") +
  genetic[match(repeat_data$id, rownames(genetic)), 1L] +
  permanent[repeat_data$id] + rnorm(nrow(repeat_data))

repeat_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", "BW", kernel = PED),
  permanent_environment = gvc("pe", "BW", kernel = gs_identity()),
  residual = gvc("residual", "BW")
)
repeat_fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id) + (1 | pe),
  data = repeat_data, vc = repeat_vcs, task = "reml",
  control = list(score_tolerance = 1e-4)
)
summary(repeat_fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(diagnostics(repeat_fit)$status$ok), isTRUE(repeat_fit$converged))
coef(repeat_fit)
head(gs_ranef(repeat_fit)$animal)
head(gs_ranef(repeat_fit)$permanent_environment)

v <- unlist(summary(repeat_fit)$covariance)
repeat_parameters <- c(v,
  heritability = unname(v["animal"] / sum(v)),
  repeatability = unname((v["animal"] + v["permanent_environment"]) / sum(v)))
repeat_parameters
pe repeats the animal IDs deliberately: it identifies a separate independent effect for the same animal. Genetic effects cover the complete pedigree; identity effects cover IDs with observed records. To specify a common herd or litter effect instead, use that grouping column and an identity kernel. Each formula grouping variable must belong to exactly one descriptor.
No solver selection or starts are required here. The adapter reuses the existing component-LMM engine with CHOLMOD selected inversion. Missing starts use an equal split of fixed-effect residual variance across the three components; each supplied start overrides only its own component. formula and formulas are equivalent. For task = "solve", supply all covariance values.
This example explicitly requests an optimizer score tolerance of 1e-4. With the component default of 1e-6, this dataset reached nearly the same estimates but did not converge: likelihood-based step acceptance stalled near the optimum. The specialized repeatability optimizer also exhausted its line search at its stricter defaults. Both routes converge at the declared 1e-4 score tolerance in their respective coordinates and give matching estimates; the component fit’s implied final variance step is below \(10^{-7}\). This is a documented example setting, not an automatic retry, a changed package tolerance or proof that the stricter stopping issue has been repaired.
Multiple-component random regression remains separate work. Correlation is not inferred from matching ID columns; the next example declares it explicitly. The specialized compiled interface remains available by explicitly passing gs_fit_control() with complete starts.

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
text:
Direct and maternal genetic effects
An animal’s phenotype may depend both on its own genetic effect and on a genetic effect expressed by its dam. These are two effects for the same trait, not two response traits. Let \(a\) denote direct genetic effects and \(m\) maternal genetic effects. The model is
\[
y = X\beta + Z_d a + Z_m m + e, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}\begin{pmatrix}a\\m\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_d^2 & \sigma_{dm}\\
\sigma_{dm} & \sigma_m^2\end{pmatrix}\otimes A,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(e)=\sigma_e^2 I.
\]
Here \(Z_d\) selects the recorded animal and \(Z_m\) its dam. Both sets of genetic effects share the pedigree relationship \(A\). One gvc() descriptor declares their shared, unstructured covariance matrix. Two separate descriptors would instead impose independence between the effects.
Reuse the same 10,000-animal pedigree and the two genetic columns from the earlier multitrait simulation. This constructs an analysis workflow; the same simulation caveat applies, so it is not an exact parameter-recovery experiment. Keep records with a known dam explicitly. Unknown dams are not assigned a shared fictitious ID or silently given zero maternal contribution.
maternal_data <- data_long[c("id", "sex", "cohort", "herd")]
maternal_data$dam <- pedigree$dam[match(maternal_data$id, pedigree$id)]
maternal_data <- droplevels(maternal_data[!is.na(maternal_data$dam), ])
stopifnot(nrow(maternal_data) > 0L)
genetic_pair <- multi_view$truth$latent_animal_values
set.seed(205)
maternal_data$BW <- 2 + 0.2 * (maternal_data$sex == "M") +
  genetic_pair[match(maternal_data$id, rownames(genetic_pair)), 1L] +
  genetic_pair[match(maternal_data$dam, rownames(genetic_pair)), 2L] +
  rnorm(nrow(maternal_data))

maternal_vcs <- list(
  genetic = gvc(
    variable = c(direct = "id", maternal = "dam"),
    traits = "BW", kernel = PED
  ),
  residual = gvc("residual", "BW")
)
maternal_fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id) + (1 | dam),
  data = maternal_data, vc = maternal_vcs, task = "reml"
)
summary(maternal_fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(maternal_fit$status$ok), isTRUE(maternal_fit$converged))
coef(maternal_fit)
G_hat <- maternal_fit$covariance$genetic
G_hat
cov2cor(G_hat)
maternal_fit$covariance$residual
head(gs_ranef(maternal_fit)$genetic)
head(data.frame(observed = maternal_data$BW,
  fitted = fitted(maternal_fit), residual = residuals(maternal_fit)))
The checked run (gsuite 0.42.0, gsim 0.9.0, seeds above) retained 14,844 records with known dams and all 10,000 pedigree animals. It converged using the default controls; the largest absolute natural score was \(4.44\times10^{-7}\).

The names direct and maternal label covariance rows, columns and prediction columns. The values id and dam select data columns. Predictions retain one row per pedigree animal, including animals without their own records. Their precision depends on available information; a fitted correlation alone is not evidence that the data identify both effects well.
Omitted starts use equal diagonal variance shares and zero initial covariance. To supply starts, pass a positive-definite matrix to the genetic descriptor, with row and column names in c("direct", "maternal") order, and a scalar residual start. task = "solve" requires both. Independent scalar components, such as maternal permanent environment or litter, can be added as separate descriptors with distinct grouping columns. The adapter currently requires known IDs in every channel for observed responses, one response trait and a residual specification described below. title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
text:
Residual variance and correlation
The residual describes variation left after fixed and random effects. We may need different residual variances for different groups, or correlation between repeated records from the same animal. These choices belong in the residual gvc() descriptor; they do not change the meaning of the animal effect.
This section reuses the 10,000-animal pedigree and repeated-record data. The following simulation helper draws only small residual blocks (two to four records per animal). The inherited genetic draws retain the earlier simulation caveat. These are separate illustrative datasets, not a model-selection study.
residual_data <- data_long[c("id", "sex", "cohort", "herd", "time")]
residual_data$occasion <- ave(residual_data$time, residual_data$id,
  FUN = function(t) c(0L, 1L, 3L, 5L)[rank(t, ties.method = "first")])
residual_mean <- 2 + 0.2 * (residual_data$sex == "M") + 0.1 * residual_data$time +
  genetic[match(residual_data$id, rownames(genetic)), 1L]
draw_residuals <- function(data, structure = "independent", parameter = NULL) {
  sd <- sqrt(ifelse(data$sex == "F", 0.6, 1.4))
  if (structure == "independent") return(sd * rnorm(nrow(data)))
  answer <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (rows in split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$id)) {
    position <- if (structure == "ar1") data$occasion[rows] else data$time[rows]
    distance <- abs(outer(position, position, `-`))
    correlation <- if (structure == "ar1") parameter^distance else exp(-parameter * distance)
    answer[rows] <- sd[rows] * as.vector(t(chol(correlation)) %*% rnorm(length(rows)))
  }
  answer
}
residual_formula <- BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + time + (1 | id)

Different residual variances by group
Set group = "sex" to estimate a residual variance for each observed sex label. This means \(\operatorname{Var}(e_i)=\sigma^2_{e,g(i)}\) and residuals remain independent across records. Sex can appear both as a fixed effect on the mean and as a residual variance group; those are separate assumptions.
set.seed(206)
residual_data$BW <- residual_mean + draw_residuals(residual_data)
grouped_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc("residual", "BW", group = "sex")
)
grouped_fit <- gfit(formula = residual_formula, data = residual_data,
  vc = grouped_vcs, task = "reml")
summary(grouped_fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(grouped_fit$status$ok), isTRUE(grouped_fit$converged))
grouped_fit$covariance$residual
Variance estimates are named by the group labels, so their interpretation does not depend on factor-level or input-row order. An optional start such as start = c(F = 0.6, M = 1.4) is matched by name. One unnamed scalar supplies the same initial value to all groups; it does not constrain their estimates to be equal. Unused levels have no estimable residual variance.


Correlation between discrete occasions
For an AR(1) residual, records within a block have correlation \(\rho^{|t_i-t_j|}\), where occasions are integers and \(-1<\rho<1\). Different blocks are independent. Gaps are retained: occasions 1 and 3 are two steps apart, even if occasion 2 is missing.
set.seed(207)
residual_data$BW <- residual_mean + draw_residuals(residual_data, "ar1", 0.45)
ar1_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc("residual", "BW", group = "sex",
    structure = "ar1", block = "id", time = "occasion")
)
ar1_fit <- gfit(formula = residual_formula, data = residual_data,
  vc = ar1_vcs, task = "reml")
summary(ar1_fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(ar1_fit$status$ok), isTRUE(ar1_fit$converged))
ar1_fit$covariance$residual$variance
ar1_fit$covariance$residual$rho


Correlation over irregular times
For exponential residuals, correlation is \(\exp(-\phi|t_i-t_j|)\) with positive decay \(\phi\). Larger decay means correlation disappears faster. The unit of time matters: changing from years to days changes the decay parameter.
set.seed(208)
residual_data$BW <- residual_mean + draw_residuals(residual_data, "exponential", 3)
exponential_vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc("id", "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc("residual", "BW", group = "sex",
    structure = "exponential", block = "id", time = "time")
)
exponential_fit <- gfit(formula = residual_formula, data = residual_data,
  vc = exponential_vcs, task = "reml", control = list(score_tolerance = 1e-4))
summary(exponential_fit)
stopifnot(isTRUE(exponential_fit$status$ok), isTRUE(exponential_fit$converged))
exponential_fit$covariance$residual$variance
exponential_fit$covariance$residual$phi
head(gs_ranef(exponential_fit)$animal)
head(data.frame(observed = residual_data$BW, fitted = fitted(exponential_fit),
  residual = residuals(exponential_fit)))
Omit group for one residual variance. Correlated blocks must each belong to one variance group and cannot contain duplicate positions; these structures have no added measurement-error nugget. Missing responses are removed together with their metadata, without compressing the remaining time gaps. The current formula route requires one response and random intercepts; combining these descriptors with random regression or multiple response traits remains separate work. Existing specialized interfaces retain their own capabilities.
The exponential example explicitly uses optimizer score tolerance 1e-4. The component optimizer tests the transformed score, not the displayed natural score. At the default 1e-6 and at 1e-5, the checked dataset did not declare convergence: the largest transformed score was \(1.13\times10^{-5}\), while the largest natural score was \(3.84\times10^{-6}\) and the implied remaining parameter step was below \(5\times10^{-8}\). This near-optimum stopping limitation remains visible, rather than being treated as a successful default fit. There is no automatic retry or package-wide tolerance change.
All three examples omit starts and use CHOLMOD selected inversion. Automatic variance starts split fixed-effect residual variance over the random channels and one residual contribution, assigning the residual share to each group. AR(1) starts at zero correlation. Exponential correlation starts at 0.2 across the median positive adjacent within-block time gap, following the existing engine. For explicit correlated starts use, for example, start = list(variance = c(F = 0.6, M = 1.4), rho = 0.3) or replace rho with a positive phi. REML can initialize omitted entries; a fixed solve requires every variance and correlation/decay parameter. Correlation and decay are reported separately from variances and must not be added to a variance sum.


Results from the checked examples
All three residual examples used 25,589 records and the same 10,000-animal pedigree (gsuite 0.42.0, gsim 0.9.0, seeds 206–208). They converged with the controls shown above. These estimates come from different simulated residual datasets, so this table does not compare the fit of competing models to one dataset.

title: Pedigree analysis with R data frames
text:
Scope and reproducibility
These examples demonstrate a workflow, not recovery of simulated covariance truth. The existing gsim generator reports exact_relationship_draw = FALSE; its recursive genetic draws and residual scaling must not be treated as an exact draw from the fitted pedigree covariance model.
General formula fits support the three specialized pedigree models above and independent pedigree/identity component groups, including explicitly correlated channels for one response. Unsupported combinations are rejected. Explicit compiled controls retain the specialized compiled-MME contract; see Formula REML. Covariance descriptors remain the extension point; these examples do not claim support for every LMM or for large-data adapters.
If the iteration limit is reached, inspect diagnostics and the model first. An explicit control = c(fit_control, list(maximum_iterations = 80L)) requests more iterations for a subsequent fit. No retry or tolerance relaxation occurs automatically. The convenience interface otherwise uses the existing route-specific controls with sparse direct solving. Success on these examples does not establish full platform qualification or reproduce the separately recorded benchmark runs.
Developers can run these exact R blocks with Rscript --vanilla tools/examples/run_pedigree_workflow.R. The runner uses an installed gsuite, records package versions, seeds, statuses and session details under ignored build/examples/pedigree-workflow/, and fails if any REML example does not converge. The website never reads that directory. The original larger pedigree benchmark evidence and its evidence are retained separately.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text:
gsuite provides an explicit, experimental R interface to the gsolve, greml, and gbits native libraries. It is deliberately below a formula or data-frame layer: callers supply fixed-effect matrices, covariance components, response order, BED dimensions, and numerical controls directly.


bed <- gs_bed("cohort.bed", n_samples = 100, n_markers = 1000)
model <- gs_model(
  fixed = cbind(intercept = 1, age = age),
  covariance = list(gs_genomic(bed), gs_residual()),
  method = "reml",
  route = "matrix_free"
)
fit <- gs_model_fit(
  model,
  response = y,
  start = c(genetic = 0.5, residual = 0.5),
  control = gs_control(threads = 4, multiple_rhs = "block")
)
summary(fit)
gs_bed() uses explicit physical dimensions and does not parse BIM or FAM files. Optional sample and marker selections are one-based, unique, ordered R indices. They are checked once and converted to the zero-based native contract. The selected order is preserved. Genotype dosage orientation and missing-call decoding are inherited from gbits.
The BED object owns immutable prepared packed storage, its selection, and its transformation. It supports raw, centered, scaled, and centered-scaled transforms and the public gbits missing policies. Centered-scaled mean imputation is the default. Marker weights are nonnegative, and genomic normalization is explicitly positive; by default it is the sum of weights. The matrix-free route uses gbits::gsolve_adapter and never forms a dense GRM.



gs_bed, gs_model, and gs_fit are ordinary R lists containing registered, finalized native handles. Copying an R object shares its immutable native handle. Compiled models retain their BED operators, and fits retain their compiled model and response, so correctness does not depend on R garbage- collection order. Each fit or post-fit inference request creates an independent mutable greml::ModelWorkspace; stale workspace state is not reused.
Handles are process-local and are not serialized for reuse across R sessions. Save the explicit BED path, dimensions, selections, and model specification and reconstruct handles in a new process. Users never manage raw addresses.



The ordered-parent gs_model_pedigree() constructor below serves the persistent model workflow. The data-frame gs_pedigree() constructor serves the separate formula workflow; neither dispatches to the other. See qualification limits for the focused repair verification and remaining package limitations.
gs_dense_covariance() supplies a finite symmetric dense component. gs_genomic() supplies a prepared matrix-free genomic component. gs_residual() supplies identity residual covariance or a known positive diagonal. Residual weights are relative covariance diagonal values multiplied by the fitted residual variance; they are not precisions.
gs_group() takes one positive one-based group index per observation. It keeps declared level order, permits unobserved trailing levels through n_levels, and treats optional positive level_weights as relative level variances. The native implementation uses an independent-group operator or sparse incidence term and does not construct an R incidence matrix.
gs_model_pedigree() takes ordered one-based parent references. NA_integer_ and zero mean unknown; every known parent must precede its offspring, and gsuite does not reorder pedigrees. observation_animal supports animals without records and repeated records. Caller-supplied Mendelian variances must be positive. When absent, greml’s public pedigree helper derives them using zero supplied inbreeding coefficients. Matrix-free paths use pedigree recursion and sparse paths use Henderson contributions; neither dense A nor dense \(A^{-1}\) is formed.
gs_sparse_random() copies the complete CSC slots of a Matrix::dgCMatrix. It represents \(Z Q^{-1} Z^{\mathsf T}\), preserving coefficient-column order. precision is the positive diagonal of Q; alternatively, level_weights are positive relative coefficient variances and are inverted once to form diagonal Q. Identity and positive diagonal precision are supported by this constructor.



gs_model() inserts no intercept, drops no columns, and performs no rank repair. fixed = NULL means zero fixed-effect columns. Exact dense and matrix-free stochastic, sparse-MME, and hybrid routes are selected explicitly. Dense components are rejected by matrix-free and sparse routes. Sparse MME is currently REML-only and accepts structured terms plus exactly one residual. Hybrid models accept structured terms, one residual, and prepared genomic matrix-free terms. The native hybrid parameter order is structured terms, residual, then matrix-free terms; declared_components records caller order when this canonical order differs. Named starts avoid ambiguity.
Sparse-MME fixed-parameter evaluation returns exact coefficient-space solves, REML likelihood, and determinant ingredients. Its optimizer uses greml’s stochastic score machinery while retaining the exact sparse likelihood. A fixed-parameter hybrid call returns projection solves and predictions but no likelihood through the current facade; hybrid likelihood and optimization diagnostics are available through the stochastic optimizer path. Hybrid optimization is REML-only. No route is selected automatically.
Group, pedigree, and general sparse terms can also enter an ordinary matrix-free covariance sum. Hybrid construction pairs the structured sparse system with remaining matrix-free operators and prevents concurrent outer use of its shared sparse factorization. Use one outer thread and operator-local threads for prepared BED work.
A compiled model can be reused with compatible response vectors and starting parameters. Sparse symbolic analysis is performed once per independent fit workspace and reused across its numerical refactorizations; separate fits use separate mutable workspaces by design.



gs_control() exposes requested threads and seed; covariance and fixed-normal PCG tolerances; independent or true block multiple-RHS solves; automatic, identity, Jacobi, sparse-structured, or caller-basis two-level preconditioning; probe count, batching and Lanczos depth; adaptive precision caps; reference or safeguarded optimization; and bounded history, prediction, and uncertainty requests. Defaults are compact development settings, not universal production recommendations.
Invalid input and structural setup failures are R errors. Legitimate optimizer nonconvergence, iteration exhaustion, stochastic-precision failure, and linear-solve precision failure remain structured fit results (with an optional warning). diagnostics() keeps optimizer, Monte Carlo precision, linear-solve, preconditioner, execution, and linked-library information distinct. Matrix-free diagnostics include the preparation, response, and information PCG batches, per-column iteration and true-residual records, operator and preconditioner applications, processed columns, and block-PCG rank/activity counters rather than only aggregate wall time.
gs_ranef() returns named coefficient blocks in structured-term order. Sparse MME exposes group, pedigree, and general sparse-Z coefficient predictions. The current hybrid facade exposes coefficient predictions only for general sparse-Z terms; observation-space component predictions remain available for every hybrid component. fitted() excludes the declared residual component, and residuals() returns response minus those fitted values.
vcov(fit, type = "covariance") returns covariance-parameter uncertainty when available. type = "fixed" returns the full fixed-effect covariance only when formed; iterative large-p projection reports explicit unavailability instead of returning an empty matrix. gs_contrast() supports selected fixed-effect inference, including iterative contrast solves. gs_wald() supports fixed or covariance-parameter hypotheses and deliberately does not add p-values.



gs_multivariate_index() preserves caller row order and accepts each unit-trait pair at most once. Missing phenotypes are absent pairs. It records trait-local row positions, counts, declared dimensions, and balanced-complete status. gs_longitudinal_index() adds explicit one-based occasion indices and finite times; unit-trait pairs may repeat at distinct occasions, but a unit-trait-occasion triple is unique. Times are neither sorted nor transformed.
gs_trait_covariance() supports fixed full covariance, fixed positive diagonal covariance, a caller-supplied lower Cholesky factor, and optimized packed log-Cholesky coordinates. Packed order is column-major lower order: (1,1), (2,1), ..., (q,1), (2,2), .... Diagonal Cholesky coordinates are exponentiated, so optimized covariances are strictly SPD and are never silently projected to a PSD boundary.
gs_multivariate_model() combines unit-level dense, group, pedigree, sparse, or prepared-genomic operators with small trait covariances through greml’s indexed observed-principal-submatrix operator. It constructs neither a dense Kronecker matrix nor a global dense residual. Trait-specific fixed matrices follow index$trait_positions; global coefficient order is trait order and then caller column order. Global names use traitN: prefixes while local names remain in model metadata. Complete prediction order is unit + (trait - 1) * n_units in one-based R notation.
gs_random_regression() accepts a caller-supplied observation-by-basis matrix, a unit covariance, and a covariance over trait-by-basis axes. Latent order is unit + (((trait - 1) * n_basis + basis - 1) * n_units). The package does not generate polynomial or spline bases. gs_longitudinal_residual() exposes independent occasions, compound symmetry, discrete AR(1), continuous-time AR(1), and heterogeneous discrete AR(1). Its correlation argument is the native unconstrained transformed coordinate: logistic for compound symmetry, tanh for discrete AR(1), and log decay for continuous AR(1).
Both families use the existing persistent gs_model/gs_fit handles and fresh workspaces. Exact-dense and matrix-free stochastic routes are explicit. Prepared genomic bases require matrix-free inference and form no dense GRM. predict() returns observed contributions, complete_predictions retains complete multivariate targets, gs_ranef() returns longitudinal latent coefficients, and gs_selected_prediction() performs bounded one-based target inference. Covariance summaries, genetic correlations, delta-method uncertainty when requested, Monte Carlo precision, and solver diagnostics stay separate.



This interface does not provide formulas, automatic intercepts or contrasts, data-frame alignment, BIM/FAM parsing, allele flipping, genome-build conversion, arbitrary sparse coefficient precision, automatic route selection, selected-inverse uncertainty, or public binary distribution. A pedigree and genomic term in one hybrid model are separate covariance components and are not an automatic single-step H or \(H^{-1}\) construction. Windows local installation is a maintainer/development workflow requiring access to the sibling native repositories. The matched binary workflow currently produces private validation bundles, not public installation downloads. This persistent-model interface does not expose the specialized sparse pedigree MME fitters described in the following sections; those have separate public R constructors and fit functions. Complete-grid prediction is provided for cross-sectional multivariate terms; longitudinal prediction targets are explicit latent basis coefficients rather than an implicit time grid.
The historical native set for this interface description was gsolve 0.21.0 ABI 3, greml 0.48.0 ABI 20, and gbits 0.21.0 ABI 4 with its gsolve adapter. For current build requirements use package metadata, not that historical set. Package loading queries the actual libraries and requires compatible ABIs and adapter linkage. These checks do not promise a stable native C++ ABI.



gs_multitrait_pedigree_records() represents only observed scalar traits and groups them into residual-independent observation units. gs_multitrait_pedigree_fit() supports fixed-SPD sparse-PCG MME/BLUP and fixed-parameter exact or stochastic REML. Covariance optimization supports complete deterministic coefficient traces under an explicit dimension limit or the qualified fixed-common-probe stochastic PCG route. The result distinguishes covariance-optimizer status, optional likelihood availability, BLUP finalization, logical PCG systems and recovered retries; an imprecise final SLQ estimate remains diagnostic and does not invalidate converged covariance or retained BLUP. See the dedicated interface note.



gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records() represents one observed scalar record per row with a pedigree animal, supplied fixed and random-regression basis rows, time for reporting, and a residual-group label. Missing occasions are absent. gs_longitudinal_pedigree_fit() supports portable fixed-covariance PCG BLUP or bounded exact-trace positive-interior PARDISO REML, returning all-animal latent coefficients plus observed and supplied prediction trajectories. The direct route has explicit coefficient, trace, batch and factor-memory limits and no silent PCG fallback. See the dedicated interface note.
All three pedigree REML controls expose exact_trace_method = "coordinate" | "selected_inverse" and maximum_selected_inverse_workspace_bytes. Coordinate traces remain the default. Selected inversion requires an explicitly resolved serial CHOLMOD factor, performs one derivative-support inverse request per full accepted-state trace evaluation, and leaves AI derivative-response solves unchanged. PARDISO, including automatic resolving to PARDISO, returns not_supported; neither the backend nor trace method falls back. The common sparse_direct$selected_inverse_trace diagnostics report requested/resolved method, capability and message, derivative/request/factor entry counts, workspace and projected peak bytes, calls/successes/failures, coordinate systems avoided, support threads, numerical validity, and retained-factor validity.
For a route-by-route numerical and statistical overview, see gsolve and greml capabilities. The bounded read-only dataset campaign and its explicit nonconvergence outcomes are recorded in qgdata qualification.

Sparse MME is currently REML-only and accepts structured terms plus exactly one residual. Hybrid models accept structured terms, one residual, and prepared genomic matrix-free terms. The native hybrid parameter order is structured terms, residual, then matrix-free terms; declared_components records caller order when this canonical order differs. Named starts avoid ambiguity.
Sparse-MME fixed-parameter evaluation returns exact coefficient-space solves, REML likelihood, and determinant ingredients. Its optimizer uses greml’s stochastic score machinery while retaining the exact sparse likelihood. A fixed-parameter hybrid call returns projection solves and predictions but no likelihood through the current facade; hybrid likelihood and optimization diagnostics are available through the stochastic optimizer path. Hybrid optimization is REML-only. No route is selected automatically.
Group, pedigree, and general sparse terms can also enter an ordinary matrix-free covariance sum. Hybrid construction pairs the structured sparse system with remaining matrix-free operators and prevents concurrent outer use of its shared sparse factorization. Use one outer thread and operator-local threads for prepared BED work.
A compiled model can be reused with compatible response vectors and starting parameters. Sparse symbolic analysis is performed once per independent fit workspace and reused across its numerical refactorizations; separate fits use separate mutable workspaces by design.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text:
gs_control() exposes requested threads and seed; covariance and fixed-normal PCG tolerances; independent or true block multiple-RHS solves; automatic, identity, Jacobi, sparse-structured, or caller-basis two-level preconditioning; probe count, batching and Lanczos depth; adaptive precision caps; reference or safeguarded optimization; and bounded history, prediction, and uncertainty requests. Defaults are compact development settings, not universal production recommendations.
Invalid input and structural setup failures are R errors. Legitimate optimizer nonconvergence, iteration exhaustion, stochastic-precision failure, and linear-solve precision failure remain structured fit results (with an optional warning). diagnostics() keeps optimizer, Monte Carlo precision, linear-solve, preconditioner, execution, and linked-library information distinct. Matrix-free diagnostics include the preparation, response, and information PCG batches, per-column iteration and true-residual records, operator and preconditioner applications, processed columns, and block-PCG rank/activity counters rather than only aggregate wall time.
gs_ranef() returns named coefficient blocks in structured-term order. Sparse MME exposes group, pedigree, and general sparse-Z coefficient predictions. The current hybrid facade exposes coefficient predictions only for general sparse-Z terms; observation-space component predictions remain available for every hybrid component. fitted() excludes the declared residual component, and residuals() returns response minus those fitted values.
vcov(fit, type = "covariance") returns covariance-parameter uncertainty when available. type = "fixed" returns the full fixed-effect covariance only when formed; iterative large-p projection reports explicit unavailability instead of returning an empty matrix. gs_contrast() supports selected fixed-effect inference, including iterative contrast solves. gs_wald() supports fixed or covariance-parameter hypotheses and deliberately does not add p-values.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text:
gs_multivariate_index() preserves caller row order and accepts each unit-trait pair at most once. Missing phenotypes are absent pairs. It records trait-local row positions, counts, declared dimensions, and balanced-complete status. gs_longitudinal_index() adds explicit one-based occasion indices and finite times; unit-trait pairs may repeat at distinct occasions, but a unit-trait-occasion triple is unique. Times are neither sorted nor transformed.
gs_trait_covariance() supports fixed full covariance, fixed positive diagonal covariance, a caller-supplied lower Cholesky factor, and optimized packed log-Cholesky coordinates. Packed order is column-major lower order: (1,1), (2,1), ..., (q,1), (2,2), .... Diagonal Cholesky coordinates are exponentiated, so optimized covariances are strictly SPD and are never silently projected to a PSD boundary.
gs_multivariate_model() combines unit-level dense, group, pedigree, sparse, or prepared-genomic operators with small trait covariances through greml’s indexed observed-principal-submatrix operator. It constructs neither a dense Kronecker matrix nor a global dense residual. Trait-specific fixed matrices follow index$trait_positions; global coefficient order is trait order and then caller column order. Global names use traitN: prefixes while local names remain in model metadata. Complete prediction order is unit + (trait - 1) * n_units in one-based R notation.
gs_random_regression() accepts a caller-supplied observation-by-basis matrix, a unit covariance, and a covariance over trait-by-basis axes. Latent order is unit + (((trait - 1) * n_basis + basis - 1) * n_units). The package does not generate polynomial or spline bases. gs_longitudinal_residual() exposes independent occasions, compound symmetry, discrete AR(1), continuous-time AR(1), and heterogeneous discrete AR(1). Its correlation argument is the native unconstrained transformed coordinate: logistic for compound symmetry, tanh for discrete AR(1), and log decay for continuous AR(1).
Both families use the existing persistent gs_model/gs_fit handles and fresh workspaces. Exact-dense and matrix-free stochastic routes are explicit. Prepared genomic bases require matrix-free inference and form no dense GRM. predict() returns observed contributions, complete_predictions retains complete multivariate targets, gs_ranef() returns longitudinal latent coefficients, and gs_selected_prediction() performs bounded one-based target inference. Covariance summaries, genetic correlations, delta-method uncertainty when requested, Monte Carlo precision, and solver diagnostics stay separate.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text:
This interface does not provide formulas, automatic intercepts or contrasts, data-frame alignment, BIM/FAM parsing, allele flipping, genome-build conversion, arbitrary sparse coefficient precision, automatic route selection, selected-inverse uncertainty, or public binary distribution. A pedigree and genomic term in one hybrid model are separate covariance components and are not an automatic single-step H or \(H^{-1}\) construction. Windows local installation is a maintainer/development workflow requiring access to the sibling native repositories. The matched binary workflow currently produces private validation bundles, not public installation downloads. This persistent-model interface does not expose the specialized sparse pedigree MME fitters described in the following sections; those have separate public R constructors and fit functions. Complete-grid prediction is provided for cross-sectional multivariate terms; longitudinal prediction targets are explicit latent basis coefficients rather than an implicit time grid.
The historical native set for this interface description was gsolve 0.21.0 ABI 3, greml 0.48.0 ABI 20, and gbits 0.21.0 ABI 4 with its gsolve adapter. For current build requirements use package metadata, not that historical set. Package loading queries the actual libraries and requires compatible ABIs and adapter linkage. These checks do not promise a stable native C++ ABI.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text: gs_multitrait_pedigree_records() represents only observed scalar traits and groups them into residual-independent observation units. gs_multitrait_pedigree_fit() supports fixed-SPD sparse-PCG MME/BLUP and fixed-parameter exact or stochastic REML. Covariance optimization supports complete deterministic coefficient traces under an explicit dimension limit or the qualified fixed-common-probe stochastic PCG route. The result distinguishes covariance-optimizer status, optional likelihood availability, BLUP finalization, logical PCG systems and recovered retries; an imprecise final SLQ estimate remains diagnostic and does not invalidate converged covariance or retained BLUP. See the dedicated interface note.

title: Persistent explicit R interface
text:
gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records() represents one observed scalar record per row with a pedigree animal, supplied fixed and random-regression basis rows, time for reporting, and a residual-group label. Missing occasions are absent. gs_longitudinal_pedigree_fit() supports portable fixed-covariance PCG BLUP or bounded exact-trace positive-interior PARDISO REML, returning all-animal latent coefficients plus observed and supplied prediction trajectories. The direct route has explicit coefficient, trace, batch and factor-memory limits and no silent PCG fallback. See the dedicated interface note.
All three pedigree REML controls expose exact_trace_method = "coordinate" | "selected_inverse" and maximum_selected_inverse_workspace_bytes. Coordinate traces remain the default. Selected inversion requires an explicitly resolved serial CHOLMOD factor, performs one derivative-support inverse request per full accepted-state trace evaluation, and leaves AI derivative-response solves unchanged. PARDISO, including automatic resolving to PARDISO, returns not_supported; neither the backend nor trace method falls back. The common sparse_direct$selected_inverse_trace diagnostics report requested/resolved method, capability and message, derivative/request/factor entry counts, workspace and projected peak bytes, calls/successes/failures, coordinate systems avoided, support threads, numerical validity, and retained-factor validity.
For a route-by-route numerical and statistical overview, see gsolve and greml capabilities. The bounded read-only dataset campaign and its explicit nonconvergence outcomes are recorded in qgdata qualification.

title: Pedigree PEV, reliability, and trajectory uncertainty
text:
Pedigree PEV, reliability, and trajectory uncertainty
The pedigree controls accept prediction_error = "none" (the default), "selected_inverse", or "selected_solve". Exact uncertainty is available for the single-trait, incomplete-multitrait, and longitudinal pedigree interfaces when a compatible accepted sparse-direct factor is retained. selected_inverse remains CHOLMOD-only. selected_solve is qualified for PARDISO and may be used with CHOLMOD for parity.
The example assumes prepared single-trait records and a supported PARDISO build. Omitted starts use the existing initializer.
control <- gs_pedigree_reml_control(
  linear_solver = "sparse_direct",
  direct_backend = "pardiso",
  prediction_error = "selected_solve",
  prediction_error_animals = c("animal-17", "animal-3"),
  maximum_prediction_error_target_systems = 64L,
  prediction_error_rhs_batch_size = 8L,
  maximum_prediction_error_entries = 4096L,
  maximum_prediction_error_memory_bytes = 8 * 1024^3)
fit <- gs_pedigree_fit(records, control = control)
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit$status$ok), isTRUE(fit$optimizer_converged),
  isTRUE(fit$prediction_error$status$ok),
  identical(fit$prediction_error$availability, "available"))
fit$prediction_error[c("prediction_error_variance", "reliability")]
The result is conditional plug-in uncertainty from the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME. Single-trait reliability uses the pedigree kernel’s animal-specific \(A_{ii}=1+F_i\). Multitrait output contains full within-animal covariance blocks. Longitudinal output contains coefficient blocks and PEV, SEP, prior variance, reliability, and accuracy for observed and prediction basis rows in caller order.
For a single-trait animal effect, the reported quantities satisfy
\[
\mathrm{Rel}_i = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{PEV}_i}{\hat\sigma_a^2 A_{ii}},
\qquad \mathrm{SEP}_i = \sqrt{\mathrm{PEV}_i},
\qquad \mathrm{Accuracy}_i = \sqrt{\mathrm{Rel}_i}.
\]
These calculations condition on the supplied or estimated covariance parameters; they do not include uncertainty from estimating those parameters. Accuracy here is a model-based quantity, not an observed correlation with known breeding values or a cross-validation result. Only roundoff-sized violations are adjusted and reported; materially invalid PEV or reliability values produce an error status.
The data-frame gfit() pedigree route accepts the corresponding named pedigree controls and retains uncertainty in diagnostics(fit)$native$prediction_error. The separate compiled route selected by gs_fit_control() currently requires prediction_error = "none". The persistent and component interfaces have their own uncertainty contracts; these pedigree settings do not apply to every gs_fit object.
For selected_solve, let T be the canonical coefficient targets implied by the requested animals and let E_T contain their coordinate columns. The native calculation solves \(CX=E_T\) in bounded column-major batches and extracts the target rows, giving exactly \(C^{-1}[T,T]\). Targets are sorted for the internal solve and mapped back to the caller’s requested animal and trait order. Duplicate or invalid targets are rejected.
This is not selected inversion. It uses ordinary documented retained-factor multi-RHS solves, and its work grows with the number \(K=\lvert T\rvert\) of target coefficient columns. Preflight reports K systems, \(\lceil K/\texttt{batch\_size}\rceil\) batches, \(K^2\) returned inverse entries, RHS workspace, returned-block workspace, projected peak workspace, configured system/entry/memory limits, factor validity, and direct/support threads. An over-limit request fails before the first target solve. Neither a dense MME nor a full dense inverse is built.
Both exact routes perform no additional symbolic analysis, numerical factorization, response solve, likelihood, trace, score, or AI evaluation. Target solves are counted separately from response, trace, and AI solves. PCG, an incompatible direct backend, or an invalid retained factor fails explicitly; there is no coordinate, stochastic, backend, or prediction-error-method fallback. CHOLMOD selected inversion remains the scalable exact route for large requested inverse closures, while PARDISO selected_solve is intended for resource-bounded target sets.

title: Canonical LMM reductions
text:
These reductions connect specialized APIs to the shared primitives in the model catalog. They are used to detect duplicate proposals: a named model that is already an exact composition or a qualified reduction is not a missing production engine.

Residual blocks of size one reduce exactly to the independent grouped- variance path.
On integer occasions and positive rho, continuous exponential correlation with \(\phi=-\log(\rho)\) equals discrete AR(1).
Missing longitudinal occasions are absent records in both correlated and independent residual representations; no balanced rows are synthesized.
Patterned multitrait residual covariance uses the principal block for the traits actually observed in a residual unit. It is not temporal residual correlation.





A zero scalar component is omitted from the active MME and restored as zero coefficients and zero prior/PEV variance in external results.
A rank-one two-channel covariance reduces to one active relationship-based latent direction while preserving an estimable orientation. Results are transformed back to the full two-channel coordinates.
Positive-definite component blocks and strictly positive residual parameters retain the positive-interior representation. Blocks larger than two do not gain a semidefinite boundary through these reductions.





Complete-MME PEV is the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME. It does not reduce to inversion of the random-only coefficient submatrix when fixed effects are estimated.
CHOLMOD selected-inverse trace and uncertainty requests reuse one retained sparse factor and the requested inverse-entry closure.
PARDISO coordinate traces reduce trace contractions to bounded batches of exact coordinate systems, but do not provide selected inversion.
PARDISO selected_solve PEV reduces requested complete-MME inverse blocks to bounded retained-factor solves \(CX=E_T\) followed by target-row extraction. It never reduces to selected inversion or a full dense inverse.
PCG coefficient solutions do not imply an exact inverse diagonal because no retained direct factor exists.




Specialized pedigree, multitrait, longitudinal, repeatability, and formula interfaces may remain useful adapters for their validated input contracts. Identity/group effects, permanent or common environment, direct/maternal covariance, and ordinary random slopes are composition recipes whenever the component-LMM scalar-record contract is sufficient. Future work should target a precise missing adapter, backend contract, or qualification cell instead of reimplementing these reductions.

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
An assistant can help identify a missing interface, component combination or numerical capability, implement it and assemble validation evidence.
Code that runs becomes a supported model only after its statistical meaning and numerical behavior have been checked.
This tutorial illustrates the development workflow through example requests. It does not implement or qualify a new model. It complements analysis with an assistant, which describes working with existing gsuite interfaces.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
section: 1. Begin with an analysis that needs more
text:
1. Begin with an analysis that needs more
You might ask:

I have repeated body-weight measurements. I want to distinguish additive genetic variation from persistent environmental differences between animals. Can my current gsuite workflow express that model? Check the existing machinery before proposing an implementation.

A candidate repeatability model is
\[
y = X\beta + Z_a a + Z_p p + e,
\]
with mutually independent random components
\[
\operatorname{Var}(a)=\sigma_a^2 A,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(p)=\sigma_p^2 I,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e)=\sigma_e^2 I.
\]
Here \(a\) is the additive genetic animal effect, \(p\) is a permanent-environment animal effect shared across that animal’s observations, and \(e\) is the record-specific residual. The fixed design \(X\) must also reflect the study, including time effects where appropriate. This model does not by itself describe changing genetic trajectories or residual serial correlation.
This model already has an explicit gvc() workflow: the repeatability example uses separate grouping columns for animal and permanent-environment effects. It records the optimizer tolerance needed for that dataset and the stricter stopping limitation. The model catalog also lists specialized and component routes. For this request, use the existing workflow; the development steps below apply when a further requirement reveals a gap.
The assistant first inspects the installed interface, implementation and evidence. If an existing supported route meets the request, the next step is an analysis script using that route. Development begins only for an identified gap, such as exposing an existing composition through a particular interface.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
2. Classify the missing piece
You might ask:

Explain exactly what is missing. Is this an R-interface change, a combination of existing components, or new numerical work? Identify what can be reused.









Gap
Typical work
Evidence needed




Missing R interface
Add validation and translate R inputs into an existing model contract
Equivalent inputs produce the same model and results as the established route


Missing composition
Connect existing relationships, covariance blocks and record mappings
The assembled covariance and fitted results agree with an independent small reference


Missing numerical capability
Implement an operator, derivative, inference step or solver capability in its owning library
Mathematical checks, numerical reference comparisons and tests of the supported parameter domain



The qgtools-style specification separates formulas, record identities, relationship kernels, covariance descriptors and the fitting task. For the example, the two animal effects share grouping IDs but have different relationships: pedigree for genetic effects and identity for permanent environment. The internal representation must preserve that distinction.
The architecture guide identifies ownership: R validation and integration belong in gsuite, mixed-model inference in greml, and numerical solvers in gsolve. Genomic data operations remain with their existing owners. The primitive registry and model reductions help identify reusable machinery.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
3. Agree on the statistical contract
Before writing code, the assistant records what the model means and which cases the proposed extension will support.
For the repeatability example, this includes the definition of an observation, the animal ID mapping, pedigree coverage, repeated-record handling, fixed effects, covariance assumptions and prediction targets. It also includes missing-data behavior, starting values and supported variance boundaries.
The study must contain information to distinguish the components. For example, with one observation per animal, a permanent-environment identity effect and an independent residual cannot be separated by their covariance contributions. A more general syntax does not resolve identifiability.
You might ask:

Write down the model assumptions, input contract and supported domain. Explain which components the data can distinguish, and identify unsupported cases before implementing the extension.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
4. Implement a small, reusable extension
You might ask:

Implement the identified gap using existing public interfaces. Preserve current behavior, keep the change within the owning libraries, and make unsupported combinations fail clearly. Include focused validation.

Develop a reviewable patch. Where possible, translate new R syntax into an existing model description and reuse its fitting algorithm.
Keep the first supported scope explicit. Missingness, covariance boundaries, prediction and uncertainty each need their own contract; successful fitting does not automatically establish support for all of them.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
5. Establish statistical and numerical evidence
For a small deterministic repeatability example, independently assemble
\[
V = \sigma_a^2 Z_a A Z_a^{\mathsf T}
  + \sigma_p^2 Z_p Z_p^{\mathsf T}
  + \sigma_e^2 I.
\]
This dense calculation is a small reference, not the production execution strategy. It lets the assistant check the model independently of the new interface or assembly code.







Check
What it establishes




Covariance and record mapping at fixed parameters
The implementation represents the stated statistical model


Likelihood and fixed-covariance predictions against the small reference
Numerical calculations agree under matched conventions


Scores and information, where applicable
Optimization quantities match independent calculations; derivative checks use appropriate interior points


REML estimates and convergence against a trusted route
The supported fitting path reaches a consistent solution within declared tolerances


Reordered IDs, repeated records and supported missingness
Input representation does not silently change the model


Invalid inputs, unidentified designs and unsupported boundaries
Failures are explicit and do not silently substitute another model


Existing affected workflows
The extension preserves previously supported behavior



Tolerances and pass criteria should be chosen before interpreting results. Likelihood comparisons must reconcile constants and parameter conventions. Simulation is useful, but a fitted estimate need not equal its generating parameter in a finite sample. Agreement between two wrappers over the same engine checks integration; it is not an independent numerical reference.
You might ask:

Show me the validation evidence, including failures and untested cases. Separate evidence for model correctness, numerical accuracy and performance.

Larger workloads and repeated timings are a separate qualification step. A successful small example establishes only its tested scope; it does not establish production-scale performance or support on other platforms.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
6. Make support explicit and reproducible
The extension becomes a supported workflow only when its declared statistical contract and relevant numerical checks are satisfied. Update the model catalog and qualification evidence for the exact model, backend and inference combination, recording remaining limitations. Follow the repository’s required build and package checks as well as focused model tests.
The completed work should contain a reviewable implementation, deterministic reference checks, updated interface documentation, and a small tutorial users can run. Record the versions used for qualification. An implemented but unqualified route must retain that distinction in its documentation.
You might ask:

Summarize what is now supported, which checks passed, what remains outside scope, and how another user can reproduce the example.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: From a scientific question to a supported model
text:
Grow capabilities through scientific use
Prefer extensions that other analyses can reuse: covariance structures, relationship mappings and inference capabilities. Scientific review and validation determine which resulting workflows gsuite can support.
crumbs: Developing a model with an assistant

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
This section defines the LMM architecture. Current dependency versions are recorded in package metadata; the original architecture baseline used greml 0.66.0. Capability status belongs in the model catalog, reusable machinery in the primitive registry, evidence in model qualification, and established equivalences in model reductions. Historical development notes do not supersede the current capability catalog.


Current public headers and R exports define what is implemented. Focused tests and committed qualification evidence determine whether a specific model/backend/inference combination is qualified. The catalog uses exactly:

qualified: implemented, publicly reachable where claimed, and covered by focused numerical or contract evidence for that combination;
implemented_unqualified: code exists, but the complete claimed combination lacks focused qualification;
unsupported: the combination rejects explicitly or has no implementation;
not_applicable: the concept does not apply to the route.

Code presence alone never establishes qualified. A limitation on one route must not be generalized to the suite.



The backend-independent specification contains caller-ordered observed records and stable record IDs; response values; compact fixed-coefficient references; random component, level, channel/trait, and basis references; deterministic external domains and coefficient order; relationship covariance or precision contracts; typed covariance layouts; residual blocks and groups; prediction targets; uncertainty requests; and separate resource/execution policy.
Caller record order may change only record-shaped output order. Scientific domains, parameter positions, likelihoods, active sets, coefficients, and uncertainty results are deterministic after alignment by external identity. Production stores short record-level coefficient-reference lists and never materializes a global fixed- or random-effect incidence matrix, dense or sparse. Pedigree routes reuse the committed ordering, inbreeding, Henderson precision, relationship diagonal, and determinant.




Component LMM coefficients are component-major, then level-major, then channel-major.
Pedigree random-regression coefficients are animal-major, then basis axis.
Pedigree multitrait coefficients retain declared trait order for every external animal.
Fixed effects retain validated caller column order.
Structured residual values use canonical variance-group order followed by rho or phi; they are not packed SPD matrices.
SPD covariance values retain declared channel/trait order and use explicit natural and log-Cholesky transformed layouts.

Every public result returns identities or names; callers do not infer them from undocumented offsets.



Scientific syntax is independent of PCG, CHOLMOD, PARDISO, batching, threading, and memory budgets. Gsolve owns numerical sessions and selected inversion; greml owns model assembly, likelihoods, derivatives, optimization, BLUP, and uncertainty; gsuite owns R validation, lowering, typed serialization, and external-order restoration.
Backend and trace method are distinct. CHOLMOD and PARDISO consume the same sparse MME, but only CHOLMOD supplies selected inversion. Coordinate traces are an exact bounded route. Retained-factor selected_solve target-block uncertainty is another exact bounded route and is not selected inversion. PCG has no retained direct factor. Stochastic Hutchinson/SLQ routes exist only where the catalog identifies them; they are never silent fallbacks for exact sparse-direct fits.
Incomplete-multitrait pedigree stochastic REML constructs deterministic counter-Rademacher trace and determinant banks once per fit and retains common probe identities across accepted and trial covariance states. Greml inference owns phase-aware precision: finite raw trace and score standard errors are diagnostics; nonstationary step resolution is assessed on curvature/Newton scales; convergence requires score compatibility with zero and adequate dimensionless log-Cholesky-scale uncertainty. Natural and transformed AI are validated and canonically symmetrized at the greml inference boundary before one identical matrix is used for rank diagnostics and the gsolve moment solve.
Stochastic covariance convergence, approximate likelihood availability, and BLUP finalization are distinct states. Final SLQ imprecision does not revoke an accepted score/AI optimum or prevent retained-response BLUP, but it makes the restricted likelihood unavailable for reporting or model comparison. Solver diagnostics likewise separate logical PCG systems from attempts, recovered warm-start retries, and unrecovered failures.
Successful direct optimization retains the accepted likelihood, factor, response, score, AI state, and relevant selected-inverse values. BLUP reuses the retained response. Exact coefficient PEV is the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME, conditional on fitted covariance parameters. Existing CHOLMOD selected inversion, pedigree trace contractions, longitudinal pedigree uncertainty, and component-LMM uncertainty are current capabilities. Exact PARDISO selected_solve PEV is qualified for the three sparse pedigree routes; PCG exact PEV and PARDISO selected inversion remain unsupported.



The component LMM’s opt-in active-set policy supports an exact zero scalar random component and rank-one two-channel covariance with KKT checks and reactivation. Larger covariance blocks and all residual parameters remain positive-interior. AR(1) and continuous exponential residual blocks share one typed residual-block abstraction; this does not imply ARMA, heterogeneous temporal scales, spatial covariance, or mixtures of residual structures.



Proposed extensions must begin with an unsupported or implemented_unqualified catalog cell, identify whether the gap is representation, exposure, backend contract, or qualification only, and reuse the registry and reductions. They must not duplicate existing solvers, selected inversion, PEV calculations, component composition, residual blocks, or boundary optimization.





The recipe defines the response, fixed terms, random components and incidence, coefficient domains, covariance and residual structures, missingness, requested predictions, identifiability conditions, and exclusions. It must not encode a backend, trace route, batch width, or memory policy.



The retained compiled route is selected with control = gs_fit_control(...); formula and formulas are aliases and do not select different routes. It requires explicit gvc() components with complete starts and no separate pedigree argument. The general data-frame adapter is described in the pedigree tutorial. For the compiled route, base R model.frame() and model.matrix() construct trait-specific fixed designs. Supported random terms are lowered recordwise as component/member, entity, trait, residual-unit, and unit-weight metadata; no R random-effect incidence matrix is constructed. Scalar lowering now composes at most one pedigree and one independent identity random-intercept domain. Formula order fixes component blocks and parameter order, while data-induced cross-domain MME entries are retained. Step resolution and convergence remain distinct. Nonstationary directions use the parameter-step covariance \(\mathrm{AI}^{-1}\Sigma_g\mathrm{AI}^{-1}\) and may extend, damp, or fail explicitly. It is not rejected merely because uncertainty divided by a vanishing proposed update is large. Trials omit SLQ and result finalization; a potentially acceptable trial is compared at a matched prefix with paired common-probe merit uncertainty. Optimizer, optional likelihood, BLUP, and solver statuses remain separate, and no adaptive route falls back to direct inference.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
Canonical LMM architecture
text:
The backend-independent specification contains caller-ordered observed records and stable record IDs; response values; compact fixed-coefficient references; random component, level, channel/trait, and basis references; deterministic external domains and coefficient order; relationship covariance or precision contracts; typed covariance layouts; residual blocks and groups; prediction targets; uncertainty requests; and separate resource/execution policy.
Caller record order may change only record-shaped output order. Scientific domains, parameter positions, likelihoods, active sets, coefficients, and uncertainty results are deterministic after alignment by external identity. Production stores short record-level coefficient-reference lists and never materializes a global fixed- or random-effect incidence matrix, dense or sparse. Pedigree routes reuse the committed ordering, inbreeding, Henderson precision, relationship diagonal, and determinant.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
Component LMM coefficients are component-major, then level-major, then channel-major.
Pedigree random-regression coefficients are animal-major, then basis axis.
Pedigree multitrait coefficients retain declared trait order for every external animal.
Fixed effects retain validated caller column order.
Structured residual values use canonical variance-group order followed by rho or phi; they are not packed SPD matrices.
SPD covariance values retain declared channel/trait order and use explicit natural and log-Cholesky transformed layouts.

Every public result returns identities or names; callers do not infer them from undocumented offsets.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text:
Scientific syntax is independent of PCG, CHOLMOD, PARDISO, batching, threading, and memory budgets. Gsolve owns numerical sessions and selected inversion; greml owns model assembly, likelihoods, derivatives, optimization, BLUP, and uncertainty; gsuite owns R validation, lowering, typed serialization, and external-order restoration.
Backend and trace method are distinct. CHOLMOD and PARDISO consume the same sparse MME, but only CHOLMOD supplies selected inversion. Coordinate traces are an exact bounded route. Retained-factor selected_solve target-block uncertainty is another exact bounded route and is not selected inversion. PCG has no retained direct factor. Stochastic Hutchinson/SLQ routes exist only where the catalog identifies them; they are never silent fallbacks for exact sparse-direct fits.
