Greml inference owns phase-aware precision: finite raw trace and score standard errors are diagnostics; nonstationary step resolution is assessed on curvature/Newton scales; convergence requires score compatibility with zero and adequate dimensionless log-Cholesky-scale uncertainty. Natural and transformed AI are validated and canonically symmetrized at the greml inference boundary before one identical matrix is used for rank diagnostics and the gsolve moment solve.
Stochastic covariance convergence, approximate likelihood availability, and BLUP finalization are distinct states. Final SLQ imprecision does not revoke an accepted score/AI optimum or prevent retained-response BLUP, but it makes the restricted likelihood unavailable for reporting or model comparison. Solver diagnostics likewise separate logical PCG systems from attempts, recovered warm-start retries, and unrecovered failures.
Successful direct optimization retains the accepted likelihood, factor, response, score, AI state, and relevant selected-inverse values. BLUP reuses the retained response. Exact coefficient PEV is the random-effect block of the inverse of the complete MME, conditional on fitted covariance parameters. Existing CHOLMOD selected inversion, pedigree trace contractions, longitudinal pedigree uncertainty, and component-LMM uncertainty are current capabilities. Exact PARDISO selected_solve PEV is qualified for the three sparse pedigree routes; PCG exact PEV and PARDISO selected inversion remain unsupported.

title: Canonical LMM architecture
text: The component LMM’s opt-in active-set policy supports an exact zero scalar random component and rank-one two-channel covariance with KKT checks and reactivation. title: Canonical LMM architecture
text: Proposed extensions must begin with an unsupported or implemented_unqualified catalog cell, identify whether the gap is representation, exposure, backend contract, or qualification only, and reuse the registry and reductions. They must not duplicate existing solvers, selected inversion, PEV calculations, component composition, residual blocks, or boundary optimization.

title: Longitudinal sparse-pedigree REML and BLUP
text:
Longitudinal sparse-pedigree REML and BLUP
gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records() stores only observed scalar longitudinal records. Each row supplies an animal, phenotype, reporting time, fixed-design row, caller-supplied random-regression basis row, and residual-group label. Missing occasions are absent rows. Records may be irregular, repeated, arbitrarily ordered, and uneven across animals; pedigree-only animals remain in the fitted domain. Character residual groups use deterministic lexical order and integer groups use deterministic numeric order, so record permutation does not change covariance-parameter positions.
ped <- gs_pedigree_data(
  individual = c("dam", "sire", "offspring", "relative"),
  sire = c(NA, NA, "sire", "sire"),
  dam = c(NA, NA, "dam", "dam")
)
animal <- c("dam", "dam", "sire", "offspring", "offspring")
time <- c(0, 1.4, 0.2, 0.7, 2.1)
y <- c(1.1, 1.8, 0.9, 1.4, 2.2)

records <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_records(
  ped, animal, y, time,
  basis = cbind(intercept = 1, time = time),
  fixed = cbind(intercept = 1, time = time),
  residual_group = ifelse(time < 1, "early", "late")
)
start <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_start(records)
control <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_reml_control(
  linear_solver = "sparse_direct", direct_backend = "pardiso",
  requested_threads = 8,
  exact_trace_method = "coordinate",
  maximum_direct_coefficient_dimension = 5000,
  max_exact_trace_systems = 5000
)
fit <- gs_longitudinal_pedigree_fit(
  records, start, covariance = "optimized", control = control,
  prediction = list(
    animal = c("offspring", "relative"), time = c(1.5, 1.5),
    basis = cbind(1, c(1.5, 1.5)),
    fixed = cbind(1, c(1.5, 1.5))
  )
)
The deterministic non-RHE start fits the supplied fixed design, calculates \(s_r^2=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{N-\operatorname{rank}(X)}\) and mean basis magnitude \(m_b=\frac{1}{N}\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert^2\), then sets \(Q_0=\frac{s_r^2}{2m_b}I\) and each residual-group variance to \(s_r^2/2\). User-supplied SPD Q and positive residual starts override it.
Both solvers use one canonical animal-major sparse MME. linear_solver = "pcg" is portable and is the large fixed-covariance BLUP route. "sparse_direct" is an optional moderate-problem route with one reused PARDISO or CHOLMOD symbolic analysis, exact retained-factor likelihood, and bounded complete coordinate traces. Automatic selection prefers PARDISO; CHOLMOD and support work are serial. Explicit direct selection never falls back: an unavailable backend returns not_supported and the gsolve message. PCG factors the bounded fixed-effect preconditioner block and one basis-rank block per pedigree animal, and verifies the true MME residual.
Coordinate traces remain the default. Explicit CHOLMOD supernodal selected inversion replaces only the exact coordinate trace systems. Deterministic positive-definite planning compiles derivative support once, then reuses one trace plan, derivative mapping, and selected-inverse workspace across covariance states. The result reports calls, selected and filled-factor entries, workspace/request/output and projected peak bytes, systems avoided, and serial selected-inverse support threads. AI derivative-response systems, exact determinant work, optimizer acceptance, and retained BLUP finalization are unchanged. CHOLMOD orchestration and support remain serial, while selected-inverse dense kernels use an independently requested oneMKL thread count. PARDISO selected inversion, including automatic when it resolves to PARDISO, is explicitly not_supported without fallback after symbolic capability resolution and before numerical factorization. PCG remains a separate fixed-covariance route with zero direct work.
The result reports starting/final covariance, fixed effects, animal-by-basis latent coefficients, observed genetic trajectories, fitted values, residuals, Py, optional prediction trajectories, covariance/optimizer diagnostics, and complete factorization/trace/AI work. Successful optimization reuses the accepted response coefficients for one BLUP finalization and performs no additional response solve. The shared typed serializer translates these diagnostics without numerical work. In the direct diagnostics, sparse_direct$requested is a logical direct-route flag, whereas requested_backend and resolved_backend are backend strings.
The historical PARDISO coordinate-trace qualification used exact coordinate traces only. Its resource preflight bounds coefficient dimension, coordinate systems, RHS batch width, workspace, and factor memory. Construction and PCG diagnostics expose the single record pass, zero optimizer record revisits, stored sparse-statistic values/nonzeros, fixed and animal preconditioner blocks, RHS width, and true residual. The existing CHOLMOD selected-inverse trace and retained-factor prediction-error paths remain available and independently qualified through this API; the historical qualification neither changed nor requalified them. Exact PEV/reliability was unavailable on those PCG and PARDISO profiles because neither retains the required CHOLMOD selected-inverse state.
PARDISO selected inversion, MUMPS, covariance boundaries, RHE, PEV/reliability on PCG or PARDISO, serial residual correlation, multiple relationship components, genomic models, marker effects, and ssGBLUP are not supported by that historical qualification profile.
Those exclusions describe the historical coordinate-trace profile. The current prediction-error contract separately supports bounded PARDISO selected_solve coefficient and trajectory uncertainty from retained factors. This does not add PARDISO selected inversion or PCG exact PEV.

title: gmat R integration
text:
The first gmat binding provides one explicit workflow:
BED/BIM/FAM → ordered BedPanel selections → disk sparse LD → LD scores
It is a thin binding to installed public gmat interfaces. gbits owns BED decoding; gmat owns resource validation, panel mappings, sparse-LD construction and disk validation, and LD-score algorithms. gsuite validates R values and translates results and errors. No genotype decoder, dense LD matrix, sparse-LD algorithm, or score algorithm is implemented in R.

title: gmat R integration
text:
Serializable objects

gsuite_bed_resource retains canonical BED/BIM/FAM paths, physical counts, and literal ordered BIM/FAM metadata.
gsuite_bed_panel retains component resources, exact selections, selected metadata, and zero-based native source mappings.
gsuite_sparse_ld retains the output prefix and five resource paths, dimensions, settings, execution mode, and disk marker sidecar. The CSR payload stays on disk.

These list-style S3 objects have no external pointers. Later operations reopen and validate paths; gsuite_sparse_ld_open() reconstructs a descriptor from a prefix in a fresh session.

title: gmat R integration
text:
Identity and ordering
Component order is list order. Components must have identical ordered (family_id, individual_id) pairs before selection. Sample identities and per-component marker IDs are resolved exactly, and requested order is preserved. Global marker order concatenates component selections. Duplicate or missing identities are errors. Nothing silently sorts chromosomes, positions, markers, samples, or alleles.
Annotation tables require explicit unique marker row names and unique column names. Their marker-ID set must equal the disk marker set; rows may be supplied in another order because gmat realigns them by exact identity. Column order is preserved.

title: gmat R integration
text:
Numerical contract
Raw PLINK dosage counts BIM allele 1 (00 → 2, 01 → missing, 10 → 1, 11 → 0). Sparse LD centres and scales observed dosage using \(p=\operatorname{mean}(g)/2\) and \(\sqrt{2p(1-p)}\); missing calls become standardized zero. Only same-chromosome pairs inside every active distance window are considered, and \(r^2\geq\texttt{r2\_threshold}\) is retained. The disk CSR stores sorted strict-upper float correlations and has an implicit unit diagonal.
Ordinary, finite-sample-corrected, partitioned, and corrected partitioned scores stream the validated disk CSR. Corrected off-diagonal contributions are \(r^2-\frac{1-r^2}{N-2}\) with N from disk metadata and are not clamped. Annotation values may be binary, overlapping, continuous, negative, or zero.
Window boundaries are inclusive and positive windows are combined. Disabling both requires explicit full-LD authorization. Disk creation validates a same- directory staging set before publication, refuses existing owned targets by default, and publishes metadata last. The gs_gprep(task = "sparseld") contract and compatibility views are specified in sparse-LD preparation.

title: gmat R integration
text:
Limitations
The binding does not harmonize alleles, flip dosage, convert genome builds, parse summary statistics, fit LD-score regressions, create dense LD, or add a general matrix class. All five files in a persistent gmat resource must remain available together.
See the gmat method catalogue for the complete native contracts.

title: Marker-QC contract
text:
gs_gfilter() is gsuite’s summary-only marker-selection operation. It accepts the strict serializable c("gs_genotypes", "Glist") descriptor produced by gs_gprep(task = "prepare") and returns a plain marker-ID vector. It does not mutate the descriptor, read packed BED genotype bytes, write BED or CSR files, decode a genotype matrix, or construct sparse LD. gmat and gbits remain unchanged owners of metadata/LD and packed-genotype operations respectively.
Marker identity is canonical chromosome/file/BIM order. Every required chromosome-wise field is checked for the same shape, and IDs must be complete and globally unique. The existing preparation validator also reopens the BIM/FAM/BED descriptors and verifies source mappings. Genotype counts must be nonnegative integers whose sum equals the exact summary population recorded by sample_source_indices_0based and provenance$summary_samples. MAF must agree with n0, n1, and n2. Thus a study-sample preparation uses that selected population rather than the complete FAM count.



Each enabled rule creates a full-length exclusion mask; the final mask is their union. NULL disables a numeric rule and FALSE disables a logical rule.

MAF excludes \(\mathrm{maf}_j\leq\texttt{maf}\); equality is excluded.
Missingness is \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{miss}}}{n_0+n_1+n_2+n_{\mathrm{miss}}}\) and excludes values strictly greater than missing; equality is retained.
HWE excludes exact-test p-values strictly less than hwe; equality is retained.
INFO excludes values strictly less than info; equality is retained.
Ambiguity excludes the exact allele pairs A/T, T/A, C/G, and G/C.
The indel/non-SNP rule retains only exact uppercase single-base A, C, G, or T for both alleles. It therefore rejects multi-base, symbolic, and lowercase encodings without silently normalizing alleles.
MHC excludes a closed interval, including both endpoints, on stored chromosome labels 6 and chr6: GRCh37 [28,477,797, 33,448,397], or GRCh38 [28,510,120, 33,480,577]. The assembly must be explicitly GRCh37 or GRCh38, supplied as an argument or in Glist$assembly; it is never guessed.

All numeric thresholds are finite scalars in [0,1]. Logical controls are nonmissing scalars. A marker-aligned INFO field is required only when INFO filtering is enabled. It may be a named numeric vector or list, but its names must be a duplicate-free exact set of prepared marker IDs. Values are reordered by identity into canonical order before the mask is calculated.



For each biallelic marker, gsuite conditions on the observed sample count and minor-allele copy count and enumerates every feasible heterozygote count with the same allele total. The two-sided p-value is the sum of conditional genotype probabilities no greater than the observed genotype probability. Probabilities within relative tolerance 1e-12 are treated as ties. This is the conventional probability-ordering exact test. Monomorphic markers receive p-value 1. All-missing or structurally invalid counts are descriptor errors; any otherwise nonfinite HWE result is conservatively excluded when HWE filtering is enabled.
qgg 1.1.6 instead uses a one-degree-of-freedom Pearson chi-square calculation. The tested version’s gfilter() also has disabled-mask hazards, relies on incomplete positional/name alignment, and subsets its combined mask incorrectly during INFO filtering. gsuite deliberately uses the exact test, complete identity validation, independent full-length masks, and an explicit default HWE threshold of 1e-12. It also freezes the documented inclusive MAF boundary.



Glist <- gs_gprep(
  study = "Reference",
  bedfiles = bedfiles,
  task = "prepare",
  nthreads = 4
)

rsids <- gs_gfilter(
  Glist,
  maf = 0.01,
  missing = 0.05,
  hwe = 1e-12,
  ambiguous = TRUE,
  indels = TRUE
)

Glist <- gs_gprep(
  Glist = Glist,
  task = "sparseld",
  rsids = rsids,
  out_prefix = "reference_ld",
  nthreads = 4
)
Preparation computes reusable summaries once. The same unchanged descriptor can be filtered under several policies, and sparse LD is subsequently built only for the selected markers.

title: Marker-QC contract
text:
gs_gfilter() is gsuite’s summary-only marker-selection operation. It accepts the strict serializable c("gs_genotypes", "Glist") descriptor produced by gs_gprep(task = "prepare") and returns a plain marker-ID vector. It does not mutate the descriptor, read packed BED genotype bytes, write BED or CSR files, decode a genotype matrix, or construct sparse LD. gmat and gbits remain unchanged owners of metadata/LD and packed-genotype operations respectively.
Marker identity is canonical chromosome/file/BIM order. Every required chromosome-wise field is checked for the same shape, and IDs must be complete and globally unique. The existing preparation validator also reopens the BIM/FAM/BED descriptors and verifies source mappings. Genotype counts must be nonnegative integers whose sum equals the exact summary population recorded by sample_source_indices_0based and provenance$summary_samples. MAF must agree with n0, n1, and n2. Thus a study-sample preparation uses that selected population rather than the complete FAM count.

title: Architecture
text:
gsuite is the unified interface to a modular family of independently versioned computational libraries. Each native library owns a narrow data, numerical, or statistical boundary and remains independently buildable. The current gsuite R package exposes the public combinations recorded in the authoritative model catalog and summary-statistic workflow; it is not necessarily a binding for every native entry point.
gsuite and gsim are the user-facing R packages. gsim generates genotype, pedigree and observation data; gsuite provides analysis interfaces. The tutorial connects them through ordinary R data frames.

Each native library owns a narrow data, numerical, or statistical boundary and remains independently buildable. The current gsuite R package exposes the public combinations recorded in the authoritative model catalog and summary-statistic workflow; it is not necessarily a binding for every native entry point.
gsuite and gsim are the user-facing R packages. gsim generates genotype, pedigree and observation data; gsuite provides analysis interfaces. The tutorial connects them through ordinary R data frames.

title: Architecture
text:
Responsibilities



Library
Responsibility
Immediate boundary




gbits
Packed genotype storage, PLINK BED access, selections, transformations, genotype products, and weighted covariance/normal operators
Does not own genomic resource metadata, general solvers, or statistical models


gmat
BED/BIM/FAM resources, ordered panels, sparse-LD construction and storage, sparse-LD algebra, and LD scores
Delegates BED decoding to gbits and does not fit LD-score regressions


gsolve
Model-independent dense, sparse, and matrix-free operators, factorizations, preconditioned conjugate gradient, probes, and stochastic log determinants
Contains no genotype, likelihood, or mixed-model semantics


greml
ML/REML covariance models, exact and stochastic inference, sparse mixed-model equations, optimization, prediction, and uncertainty
Uses gsolve for numerical primitives and does not own genotype formats


gcorr
Ordinary and partitioned single-trait, bivariate and multivariate LDSC; genetic covariance/correlation, enrichment, jackknife uncertainty, ordinary/partitioned joint sampling covariance, summary-statistic preparation, and fit/working-weight diagnostics
Consumes gmat LD scores and does not construct or store LD


gscore
Standalone specialized high-performance multi-score application directly from PLINK BED
Owns the scoring kernel, not metadata preparation, allele alignment, or general matrix operators


gsim
User-facing R simulation of genotypes, pedigrees and observation records
Owns simulation workflows; generated data can be used in gsuite analyses


glma
Native linear, binary logistic and Gaussian mixed/LOCO association plus prior-selected LOCO fitting, structure checks, calibration and offset testing
Uses installed gmat/gbits, greml and gbayes; gsuite exposes binary and quantitative-trait routes through glma(), sharing genotype reads for multiple exact linear traits and immutable preparation for LOCO traits


gmap
Native colocalisation, regional Bayesian analysis and posterior-set interpretation
Core is standalone; optional gmap::bayes uses gbayes; gsuite binds regional Bayesian fitting, ABF and component colocalisation


gbayes
Native Bayesian regression and single-/multi-effect inference
Uses gmat cross-products or prepared factors; single-/multivariate summary regression through gsuite::gbayes and regional inference through gsuite::gmap


gsuite
Unified R/native entry point and suite-level integration documentation
Binds selected gsolve, greml, gbits, gmat, gcorr, glma and gmap/gbayes capabilities and requires the gbits gsolve adapter




How the R interface connects the components
The pedigree data-frame workflow normalizes short covariance specifications and explicit gvc() components into one internal model description. Formulas define fixed and random bases, variables bind record IDs, kernels define relationships, covariance descriptors declare coordinates and optional starts, and the task selects REML or a fixed solve. The adapter owns R validation, sparse fixed-design construction and result labels; it calls the existing specialized pedigree interfaces or the public component-LMM constructors and fitters for independent groups of random intercepts. A named vector of grouping columns in one gvc() declares correlated channels sharing a pedigree or identity relationship; separate descriptors remain independent. Residual group, structure, block and time fields bind data columns to existing grouped, AR(1) and exponential component residual constructors. Missing-response filtering is shared by phenotypes, incidence and residual metadata. No new native numerical implementation or dense relationship matrix is introduced. formula and formulas are equivalent; supplied starts do not select a different route. An explicit gs_fit_control() object selects the specialized compiled interface. General sparse-direct defaults use CHOLMOD selected inversion; independent components reuse gs_lmm_control().
For gs_gprep(task = "prepare"), ownership is fixed as follows:



Responsibility
Owner




Public R interface, orchestration, serializable descriptor
gsuite


BED validation and packed genotype counts
gbits


BIM/FAM parsing, identity, metadata, and file alignment
gmat


Persistent genotype representation
Existing PLINK BED


Behavioural and scientific comparison
Read-only qgg



For gs_gprep(task = "sparseld"), gsuite validates the Glist and orchestrates selection; gmat owns sparse-LD calculation, its disk CSR, validation, and LD scores; gbits remains the packed BED path; existing BED remains the genotype store; and unchanged qgg and sblr are behavioural and consumer references.
The independent LDlist interface reuses gmat’s existing SparseLdDiskResource and native disk inspection. ldprep(Glist, reference) creates an R descriptor without copying LD files; validate_LDlist() reopens and checks it without requiring genotype inputs. gmat owns the native resource, while gsuite owns R labels, serialization and validation orchestration. No new native storage format is introduced. LD computation is delegated to the existing sparse-LD preparation route; named score preparation delegates ordinary and partitioned/corrected calculations to gmat. gsuite stores definitions and validates saved-score compatibility. Regional dense extraction belongs to gmat and reuses its streaming disk parser. gsolve supplies the full eigensystem and numerical diagnostics; gsuite binds these installed public APIs and stores reusable region caches. gmat has no new gsolve dependency. All R/Rcpp code remains in gsuite. See LD references.
gcorr now provides native adapters for these LD resources and an immutable PreparedRegionalLd shared by HESS, rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA and LAVA. gsolve verifies imported full eigensystems once; subsequent native fits reuse them while applying their own statistical component selection. The gcorr() R interface now connects these resources to ordinary/partitioned LDSC and GNOVA, independent and joint-region HESS/rho-HESS, continuous-trait LAVA point estimates, univariate tests and optional bivariate simulation inference, and SUPERGNOVA covariance. See the summary-statistic tutorial for its bounded scope.
Across these methods, result tables use explicit reference, region, annotation-category and architecture-component labels. Named h2/cov/rg matrices share one layout; method-specific uncertainty, native diagnostics and inconsistent pairwise estimates remain visible. See result conventions.
The common gcorr() interface also exposes SumHer architecture-component and reference-total h2/cov/rg. Multiple traits use the native coordinated marginal and pairwise fits, with joint fixed-weight jackknife covariance when blocks are supplied. Tagging weights are explicit and separate from architecture-weighted scores; no cross-ancestry or full upstream-software parity is implied.
Regional LAVA also accepts explicit binary-trait metadata, reusing LDlist allele frequencies for native logistic-Wald reconstruction. Observed and liability h2 remain distinct; binary/mixed pairs use the existing screening and optional bivariate simulation inference. LAVA shares each regional fit across traits and exposes partial correlations, multiple regression, explained variance and supported conditional/omnibus inference.
Native regional request lists now resolve explicitly named references and regions, reuse prepared LD, and retain labelled results or per-request errors. Joint HESS also accepts prepared regions. These are sequential native calls; every trait within a model must select the same reference, with no cross-ancestry estimator implied by the reference labels.

title: Architecture
text:
Dependencies
This graph describes current build dependencies. Each arrow points from a dependent component to a library it requires. Building gbits::gsolve_adapter is optional for gbits; when built, the adapter requires both gbits and gsolve. The current gsuite build requires the adapter. External implementation dependencies and optional OpenMP support are omitted.
flowchart LR
    gbits[gbits]
    gmat[gmat] --> gbits
    gcorr[gcorr] --> gmat
    gcorr --> gsolve
    gsolve[gsolve]
    greml[greml] --> gsolve
    adapter["gbits::gsolve_adapter"] --> gbits
    adapter --> gsolve
    gscore[gscore]
    gmap[gmap]
    gmap_bayes["gmap::bayes (optional)"] --> gbayes
    gbayes[gbayes] --> gmat
    gbayes --> gsolve
    glma[glma] --> gbayes
    glma --> greml
    glma --> gmat
    glma --> adapter
    gsuite[gsuite R package] --> gbits
    gsuite --> gmat
    gsuite --> gmap_bayes
    gsuite --> gcorr
    gsuite --> greml
    gsuite --> gsolve
    gsuite --> adapter
There is no reverse dependency from gsolve or greml to gbits. The gscore scoring implementation reads BED directly and has no suite-library dependency. Its independent build does not change its role as the ecosystem’s scoring library. gsim is a separate user-facing R package; its simulation-to-analysis workflow exchanges data with gsuite and is not a native-library dependency. gbayes is a native library using gmat and gsolve. gmap retains standalone colocalisation and provides an optional gmap::bayes companion for regional posterior workflows. Both are now installed dependencies of the experimental gsuite gmap() R interface. Only the R conversion layer lives in gsuite; fitting and posterior-set construction remain native. The R interface accepts named regions and traits, with explicit sufficient statistics and optional native parameter learning. Residual learning requires complete in-sample LD and explicit phenotype normalization. Each region is prepared once across traits, using verified cached eigenpairs when available. Traits are fitted separately, not as a joint multivariate model. Saved multi-effect evidence feeds coloc() without refitting; the standalone ABF route instead consumes aligned beta/SE summaries directly without LD. For component comparisons, LD is reread only for purity checks.
gbayes() binds native single-trait and multivariate BayesC/BayesR summary regression directly: standardized marginal effects and aligned LD are prepared by gbayes, then fitted using its existing samplers. Parameter learning, pooled posterior summaries and chain diagnostics remain native. Sparse LD can be memory-resident (parallel chains) or disk-backed (serial chains); no dense matrix or retained external pointer is introduced. The R object owns labelled, serializable results. Named trait lists reuse one LD reference; equal sample-size vectors share the same native cross-product object. Sampling dependence is explicit and separate from latent effect covariance. R checks labels and options; native gbayes owns the multivariate preparation, SPD checks, sampler, covariance/weight updates and posterior summaries. Shared annotation conversion binds native inclusion, pattern, component and variance models; R validates design labels and returns serializable native coefficient summaries and diagnostics. See the Bayesian regression workflow.
gmap_stat() is R-side input preparation for the native mapping workflow. It reconstructs marginal OLS cross-products from aligned beta/SE/n and phenotype variance. It does not align alleles, infer missing sample sizes or add a native dependency. gmap() retains the preparation provenance. The worked mapping example connects this helper to the existing native fitting and post-fit colocalisation interfaces.

title: Architecture
text:
Ownership rules

File-format decoding and packed genotype algebra belong to gbits; reusable genomic resource identity, sparse LD, and LD scores belong to gmat.
Numerical operators and solvers belong to gsolve; ML/REML model semantics and inference belong to greml.
LD-score regression and its uncertainty belong to gcorr, not gmat.
Direct multi-score BED application belongs to gscore. Its standalone design is the current implementation boundary.
The gsuite package translates explicit R values into existing public native contracts; it does not reimplement their algorithms.
New cross-library dependencies require a demonstrated contract and must follow the existing direction without introducing cycles.

title: Architecture
text:
MR through the R interface
gcorr() exposes the native GSMR, GSMR2, IVW, Egger and weighted-median components. Use task="prepare_mr" with aligned trait tables and one LDlist, then task="mr" on the serialized preparation. Selection decisions, HEIDI results, estimate units and method-specific diagnostics remain explicit. Preparation requires matched ancestry and an explicit non-overlapping-sample assertion. Numerical selection/filtering/estimation stays in gcorr; the R layer converts inputs and results. See the MR workflow.

title: Architecture
section: Covariance models through the R interface
text:
Covariance models through the R interface
gcorr_covariance() retains labelled continuous genetic covariance and full joint sampling covariance. gcorr() exposes recursive SEM, descriptive partial-correlation networks and fixed-graph GGM through the existing native gcorr fitter. Parameter tables, trait units and estimation metadata remain explicit. Fitted SEM paths and free GGM edges support native joint Wald tests. Coordinated multivariate GNOVA annotation categories and SumHer architecture components can be fitted with the same model and compared using their full cross-group jackknife covariance; overlapping categories retain their original meaning. See the covariance-model workflow.

title: Tutorials
text:
Pedigree analysis
Pedigree analysis with R data frames
Prepare a pedigree and observations, describe the model with formulas, fit it with gfit(), and inspect the results. Begin with three models using the same workflow:

Single-trait analysis: start with a simple animal model.
Multitrait analysis: model two traits and their covariance.
Longitudinal analysis: fit genetic random regression over time.

Read the shared data preparation first; the examples build on that setup. The guide also shows how to move from the short interface to explicit covariance components, then extends it to:

Repeatability: separate genetic and permanent-environment variation.
Direct and maternal effects: declare correlated genetic effects.
Residual structures: allow grouped variances and correlation over time.

title: Tutorials
text:
GWAS summary statistics
A small comparison using simulated data
Simulate two traits with gsim, run six methods, and compare genome-wide and regional estimates with known truth. Start with one dataset, then inspect estimation errors and availability across 20 additional datasets.
From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
Run a complete artificial three-trait example: prepare and reload LD, estimate genome-wide and annotation quantities, then fit regional and conditional models. Inspect summaries, plots and uncertainty while keeping outputs in one directory.
Heritability and genetic correlation with prepared LD references
Use gcorr() for ordinary and annotation-based estimates, or select named regions for local analysis. The tutorial explains inputs, overlap assumptions, results and the current R-interface boundary.
Genetic covariance models across annotations
Fit an explicit SEM or fixed graphical model to covariance summaries, then compare selected parameters across artificial annotation groups in a runnable four-trait example.
Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
Prepare candidate instruments explicitly, then use GSMR, GSMR2, IVW, Egger or weighted median. Inspect instrument selection, HEIDI decisions and uncertainty.

title: Tutorials
text:
Fine-mapping and colocalisation
Bayesian regression from summary statistics
Use gbayes() to fit BayesC/BayesR, learn effect variance, mixture weights and annotation effects, inspect native posterior summaries and reuse labelled marker effects for scoring. A gsim example uses 10,000 individuals and one saved LD reference, then extends to three traits with explicit sampling dependence and joint covariance learning.
From GWAS results to fine-mapping and colocalisation
Prepare OLS summary statistics, compare BayesC, BayesR and multi-effect marker support, then assess shared signals. A gsim example uses two disjoint cohorts of 10,000 individuals, two regions and one saved LD reference.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
You bring the scientific question and study knowledge. An assistant can help inspect data, run R code, examine diagnostics and prepare a report using gsuite.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 1. Start with the question and data
text:
1. Start with the question and data
You might ask:

I have body-weight records, sex, cohort and herd, plus a pedigree. Help me estimate additive genetic variation and predict animal effects. First inspect the data and explain any issues that affect the analysis.

The assistant checks the column meanings and measurement units with you, then inspects missing values, duplicated records, factor levels and phenotype distributions. It checks that observation IDs match the pedigree, parent IDs are represented consistently, and pedigree relationships are valid. Repeated measurements require particular attention: several records per animal may need a different model from one observation per animal.
For a reproducible demonstration, use the Prepare ordinary data frames section and the data preparation at the start of Single trait in the pedigree tutorial. That supplies pedigree and data, including BW, sex, cohort, herd and id. For your study, use your own data frames instead.
str(data)
summary(data)
colSums(is.na(data))
anyDuplicated(pedigree$id)
setdiff(data$id, pedigree$id)
table(table(data$id))
These are initial checks, not a complete data-validation procedure. The assistant records issues and proposed changes in a data-check summary. Decisions such as excluding records or recoding missing parents belong in the analysis script, with an explanation you can review.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 2. Translate the question into a model
text:
2. Translate the question into a model
You might ask:

Treat sex, cohort and herd as fixed effects. Use the pedigree for additive genetic animal effects. Explain the assumptions and show me the model code.

For the tutorial’s single-trait model:
\[
y = X\beta + Za + e,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(a)=\sigma_a^2 A,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e)=\sigma_e^2 I.
\]
Here \(A\) is the pedigree relationship matrix. The model assumes independent animal and residual effects and a common residual variance. Whether herd should be fixed, and whether additional environmental effects are needed, depends on the study design and your scientific question.
The qgtools-style separation of effects, relationships and covariance components makes each decision explicit:



Model decision
gsuite specification




Fixed effects and animal grouping
Formula


Observations and explanatory variables
data


Relationships between animals
Pedigree kernel


Genetic and residual variance components
gvc() descriptors


Estimate covariance parameters
task = "reml"



library(gsuite)

PED <- gs_pedigree(pedigree, id = "id", sire = "sire", dam = "dam")
vcs <- list(
  animal = gvc(variable = "id", traits = "BW", kernel = PED),
  residual = gvc(variable = "residual", traits = "BW")
)
Starting variances are omitted here: gsuite uses its existing deterministic initializers. The pedigree tutorial also shows the short form, which expresses the same model with fewer arguments. The assistant checks the supported model combinations before suggesting an extension; a general specification does not imply that every model is implemented.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
3. Run and examine the fit
You might ask:

Run this model, retain the script and fit, and check convergence before interpreting the estimates. Explain any failures rather than silently changing the model.

fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data,
  vc = vcs,
  task = "reml"
)

summary(fit)
fit_diagnostics <- diagnostics(fit)
fit_diagnostics$status
fit_diagnostics$converged
fit_diagnostics$initialization
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_diagnostics$status$ok),
  isTRUE(fit_diagnostics$converged))
coef(fit)
head(gs_ranef(fit)$animal)
This data-frame route defaults to CHOLMOD selected inversion and requires a build with CHOLMOD support. The check above stops the example before prediction plots and reporting if status or convergence is unsuccessful.
After checking status and convergence, examine estimates and residual patterns for unusual values or possible confounding.
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
Record failures and unavailable diagnostics alongside the results.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
section: 4. Turn the analysis into a report
text:
4. Turn the analysis into a report
You might ask:

Create a Quarto report with the data checks, model and assumptions, convergence diagnostics, variance estimates, animal predictions and residual plots. Explain what the results support and what remains uncertain.

The report uses the actual saved results. It identifies the data used, exclusions, software versions and analysis settings, and links conclusions to tables and figures. It separates predicted animal effects from observed phenotypes and avoids presenting a failed fit as a completed analysis.
The working directory can remain small:







File
Purpose




analysis.R
Data preparation, checks and model fitting


results.rds
Extracted estimates, predictions and diagnostics for reporting


report.qmd
Methods, results, figures and interpretation


session-info.txt
R and package versions



Save the reporting values rather than relying on an in-memory fit to survive between R sessions:
results <- list(
  summary = summary(fit),
  diagnostics = diagnostics(fit),
  fixed_effects = coef(fit),
  animal_effects = gs_ranef(fit)$animal,
  record_mapping = fit$record_mapping,
  fitted = fitted(fit),
  residuals = residuals(fit)
)
saveRDS(results, "results.rds")
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session-info.txt")
The conversation helps develop the analysis. The scripts, extracted results and report preserve the work so you or a colleague can inspect and reproduce it without reconstructing the conversation.

title: From conversation to a reproducible analysis
text:
Continue with more complex models
The same collaboration applies to multitrait and longitudinal analyses: discuss the question, inspect the record structure, specify effects and covariances, run a supported model and assess the results. gsuite remains an R package with explicit interfaces; no conversational service is required inside the package.

title: Formula and variance-component compiled-MME REML
text:
For the new data-frame shorthand, optional starts, fixed solves and genetic random regression, begin with Pedigree analysis. Both formula and formulas now use the same general adapter. This page documents the specialized compiled-MME route, explicitly requested with a gs_fit_control() object, complete explicit covariance starts, and task = "reml". Its result layout remains specialized. Supplying starts alone does not select it. General fits accept named controls for the selected pedigree or component fitter. Compiled controls now default to CHOLMOD selected inversion.
The data-frame gs_pedigree() constructor described here is distinct from gs_model_pedigree(), the ordered-parent constructor used by the persistent-model API. The two signatures are not interchangeable and do not dispatch implicitly.
gfit() is gsuite’s direct formula REML entry point. Model incidence comes from formulas, pedigree relationships come from gs_pedigree(), and explicit positive-interior covariance starts come from named gvc() components. The interface lowers one immutable model to greml’s public compiled-MME plan, creates one numerical session, optimizes, and finalizes BLUPs from the retained accepted response state.
PED <- gs_pedigree(pedigree, id = "id", sire = "sire", dam = "dam")

fit <- gfit(
  BW ~ sex + batch + (1 | id),
  records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("id", "BW", PED, start = 1),
    residual = gvc("residual", "BW", start = 1)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)
For multiple traits, formulas is a named list and each component start is an SPD matrix in the declared trait order. Each trait has a separate fixed-effect block. Scalar records are ordered by formula-list order and original data-row order. An NA response is absent; observed traits from the same data row form one complete or incomplete patterned residual unit. Missing fixed covariates, nonfinite observed responses, and missing pedigree identifiers are errors.


From the repository root, with gsuite installed, run:
source("tools/examples/run_single_trait_pedigree_example.R")
The complete example starts with two ordinary data frames: data has one observation per row (id, BW, factor sex, continuous covariate x); pedigree has one animal per row (id, sire, dam). It reuses the small deterministic BW formula-test illustration, not a random draw from the fitted pedigree model. Its artificial sex labels vary across records of an animal; real data should use consistent animal sex. These toy values illustrate the API, not biological inference or variance recovery.
The formula BW ~ sex + x + (1 | id) supplies fixed effects and animal incidence. A separate gs_pedigree() relationship and named animal and residual components supply covariance structure and positive starting variances. Under this model, animal covariance is the pedigree relationship times the animal variance; residuals are independent with a common variance. Repeated observations share the animal effect, with no additional permanent environment effect. Starts are not fixed variances.
IDs, not row positions, align the tables. Pedigree rows may be reordered; unknown parents use NA, while known parents must be listed. Observation IDs absent from the pedigree are errors. Animal a8 has no observations but remains in the pedigree and receives a conditional animal prediction from relatives.
summary(fit) displays covariance estimates and convergence, coef(fit) returns fixed effects, and the public fit$random_effects$animal table contains IDs and animal BLUPs (not full predicted body weights). fit$converged and fit$convergence_reason expose the stopping result. Prediction tables follow pedigree order, so compare them by ID. Prediction for new data and prediction uncertainty are not supported on this formula route.
For development verification only, select the existing isolated installation before sourcing the same example:
.libPaths(c(file.path("build", "r-library"), .libPaths()))
source("tools/examples/run_single_trait_pedigree_example.R")



The only random grammar is exactly (1 | variable). A scalar formula has one or two distinct terms, with at most one pedigree component and one independent identity component. Multitrait formulas retain one shared pedigree term. Random slopes, more than two terms, duplicate terms, ||, nesting, crossing, functions, interactions, and expressions on the grouping side are rejected. After removing the random terms, base R model.frame() and model.matrix() build the fixed design and preserve coefficient names, contrasts, factor levels, and the formula environment.
Random incidence is never materialized as an R matrix. Each observed scalar record supplies a pedigree entity ID, trait/member ID, residual unit and coordinate, and a unit random-intercept weight directly to the compiled-MME specification. This first version may materialize a dense R fixed-effect model.matrix() and therefore targets moderate in-memory data frames.



Scalar fits accept one identity component, one pedigree component, or one of each, plus one homogeneous residual component. Formula order determines the random coefficient blocks and covariance-parameter order. Pedigree levels use external pedigree order, including unphenotyped animals. Identity levels use the sorted observed character or integer domain. Every record contributes a unit weight directly to each present component, including the data-induced pedigree/identity cross block; no R incidence matrix is built.
For example, repeatability and a common-environment model use the same bounded composition rule:
ID <- gs_identity()
repeatability <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | permanent_id), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    permanent = gvc("permanent_id", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)

common_environment <- gfit(
  y ~ sex + (1 | animal_id) + (1 | environment), records,
  list(
    animal = gvc("animal_id", "y", PED, start = 0.8),
    environment = gvc("environment", "y", ID, start = 0.4),
    residual = gvc("residual", "y", start = 0.3)
  ),
  control = gs_fit_control(direct_backend = "cholmod")
)
Starts remain mandatory finite positive scalars or finite symmetric positive-definite matrices. Covariance boundaries and automatic rank repair are not attempted.
gs_fit_control() maps backend, direct/support threads, exact trace route, optimizer bounds, coefficient dimension, factor memory, selected-inverse workspace, exact trace systems, RHS workspace, and linear-solve controls directly to the public greml session. A failed preflight does not silently change backend, trace route, batch width, or solver. Diagnostics report the required and configured RHS bytes, peak RHS width, resident coefficient vectors, workspace category, limit result, overflow result, and zero numerical work after rejection.
PARDISO uses its own requested internal thread count and coordinate-exact traces. CHOLMOD uses serial support work and selected inversion. Generic support execution remains independent; an unsupported request is returned as not_supported before solver work. No GNU OpenMP layer is introduced.
The returned gs_fit owns covariance estimates, fixed effects, animal BLUPs in external pedigree order, caller-record mappings, optional fitted values, residuals and Py, score/standard-AI diagnostics, optimizer history, resource preflight, work counters, and retained-state diagnostics. print(), summary(), coef(), fitted(), residuals(), logLik(), and nobs() are provided. Record methods fail clearly when record values were omitted.
Genomic relationships, random slopes, correlated random components, more than one pedigree or identity component, multitrait repeatability, heterogeneous or serial residual covariance, covariance boundaries, PEV/reliability, prediction from new data, disk-backed data, formula dependencies, Bayesian tasks, JSON, Python, and R-side public plan/session objects remain deliberately outside this compiled-MME formula interface.

title: gs_genotypes preparation contract
text:
gs_gprep() implements the bounded "prepare" and "sparseld" tasks. For preparation, gsuite owns argument validation, orchestration, and the returned R descriptor; gmat owns strict BIM/FAM parsing and exact ordered multi-file identity; gbits owns BED header, size, offset, packed-code, and threaded count logic. The existing SNP-major PLINK BED files remain the sole persistent genotype representation. qgg is a read-only behavioural and scientific reference and is not a runtime dependency.
Sparse-LD orchestration is specified separately in sparse-LD preparation. Separate LD-score tasks, genetic-map import, GRMs, association, scoring, and other qgg tasks are not implemented by gs_gprep(). Marker filtering is provided separately by gs_gfilter(). Unknown preparation tasks fail explicitly.



Every BED/BIM/FAM vector is nonempty and has identical length. Omitted companions are derived by replacing only a final case-insensitive .bed suffix. Every path is normalized and must name an existing regular file. gbits requires the exact header 6c 1b 01 and exact size \(3+M\lceil N/4\rceil\); individual-major, truncated, and trailing-byte inputs fail.
The first FAM supplies ids and the complete physical sample order. Individual IDs are nonempty and globally unique. gmat requires every component to have the same exact ordered (family_id, individual_id) sequence; no set-only check or positional permutation is used. With ids = NULL, all samples contribute and study_ids is NULL. A supplied vector is nonempty, unique, nonmissing, fully resolved, retained in caller order, and used only as the summary sample set; ids remains complete.
Every BIM row has six fields, a nonempty chromosome and marker ID, finite nonnegative map position, positive physical position, and distinct nonempty alleles. Source marker IDs are globally unique across every supplied BIM, including unselected rows. BIM order is canonical. A supplied rsids vector is validated completely, then filtered in file/BIM order; caller order is intentionally not retained because the public descriptor remains a file-partitioned physical view. source_marker_indices_0based records every original BIM/BED index, including noncontiguous selections. BED is never rewritten.



a1 is BIM field 5 and a2 BIM field 6. Counts and frequencies always refer to copies of a1:



PLINK code
Copies of a1
Count




00
2
n2


10
1
n1


11
0
n0


01
missing
nmiss



For \(N_{\mathrm{obs}}=n_0+n_1+n_2\), the returned values are \(\mathrm{af}=\frac{2n_2+n_1}{2N_{\mathrm{obs}}}\), \(\mathrm{af}_1=\mathrm{af}\), \(\mathrm{af}_2=1-\mathrm{af}\), \(\mathrm{maf}=\min(\mathrm{af},1-\mathrm{af})\), \(\mathrm{hom}=(n_0+n_2)/N_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and \(\mathrm{het}=n_1/N_{\mathrm{obs}}\). All-missing selected markers fail with their marker ID. Empirical frequencies are not clipped: monomorphic values are exactly zero or one. This deliberately differs from the tested qgg 1.1.6 reference, whose summaryBED() clips frequencies to [0.00001, 0.99999] and substitutes 0.5 for all-missing markers.



The result is a plain list with class c("gs_genotypes", "Glist"). It carries study, normalized bedfiles/bimfiles/famfiles, complete ids, optional study_ids, n, nchr, m, chromosome/file-wise rsids, mchr, chr, pos, map, a1, a2, cpra, af, af1, af2, maf, nmiss, hom, het, n0, n1, n2, assembly = NULL, physical sample/marker mappings, format and ordering labels, and provenance. It contains neither dense genotypes nor a mandatory external pointer and therefore survives an exact saveRDS()/readRDS() round trip.
The gsim 0.16.0 development source has a native bounded BED reader for Glist-backed simulation; qgg’s getG is no longer its default. It resolves selected sample and marker IDs against FAM/BIM files, checks allele orientation, and reads selected BED blocks. A custom deterministic getG_fun remains an explicit alternative. This removes the previously described need for a new gsuite decoder, but does not imply full qgg compatibility or qualification of every cross-package combination. Check the installed gsim version before use.



gbits scans packed marker records directly. Selected original offsets are checked with 64-bit arithmetic. Threaded execution assigns deterministic static marker partitions and never calls R from workers. Temporary native storage is \(O(T\lceil N/4\rceil)\) packed bytes for T workers plus \(O(M)\) counts and selection mappings; no \(O(NM)\) decoded matrix exists.
