title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What is AI?







Term
Meaning




Artificial intelligence
The broad field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence


Machine learning and deep learning
Methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers


Generative AI
Models that generate text, code, images, audio or other content


AI assistants and agents
Systems built around generative AI that can work with users, files and tools. Agents can carry out multistep tasks



This presentation focuses on AI assistants and agents used for data analysis, method and software development, and teaching.

People use the term AI in different ways. Some think of machine learning or deep neural networks used to analyse data. Others think primarily of generative tools such as ChatGPT.
Machine learning covers methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a form of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers. Modern generative AI is largely based on deep learning, but its purpose is to generate new content rather than only produce predictions.
Assistants interact with users and may have access to files and tools. Agents can use these capabilities to carry out more complex, multistep tasks.
This presentation concerns practical AI-assisted work. Applying machine learning as the scientific method being studied is outside its scope.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
How researchers use generative AI







Activity
Examples




Writing and communication
Draft, revise, translate and shorten text


Literature work
Find relevant papers, summarise them and compare their conclusions


Data analysis
Inspect data, write code, make figures and explain results


Teaching
Develop slides, exercises, examples and explanations


Administration
Prepare emails, meeting notes, plans and reports



Writing and literature review are common entry points. The same technology can also contribute directly to mathematical, analytical and software work.

Many researchers first encounter generative AI as a writing assistant. It can also help identify literature, organise information, write analysis code and develop teaching material.
These uses still require review. Literature searches must be checked against the original sources, and scientific claims must not be accepted simply because the generated text sounds convincing.
My own use extends further into method and software development. That is the main focus of the following slides.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Areas of AI-assisted work








Area
Example output
Reusable result




Data analysis
An analysis script and report
A reproducible analysis workflow


Method development
A statistical model or algorithm
A clearly defined method with validation evidence


Software development
R and C++ code, interfaces and documentation
Tested and maintainable software components


Teaching
Slides, simulations and worked examples
Editable teaching materials



AI can help with mathematical reasoning, coding, analysis and documentation. Researchers set the scientific direction, review the decisions and determine what evidence is sufficient.

These activities are connected but distinct. A data-analysis question may reveal the need for a new statistical method. The method must then be translated into reliable software before it can be used routinely. A validated implementation can support new analyses and become a teaching example.
AI is particularly useful at the connection between mathematics and software. It can help examine equations, compare algorithms, implement them in R or C++, and prepare numerical checks. Researchers define the scientific problem, review the statistical and computational decisions, and decide what evidence is required.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Platforms developed with AI assistance







Platform
Purpose




gsuite
Statistical models, numerical computation and user interfaces


gsim
Simulation of genetic data and assessment of methods


gact
Data integration, annotation, analysis and interpretation


gteach
Shared tools and materials for teaching



AI has contributed to developing the platforms themselves. The resulting infrastructure can now support further work with AI assistants.

gtools


These platforms represent substantial outputs from AI-assisted development. The work has included mathematics, numerical algorithms, R and C++ code, interfaces, documentation, simulation, data organisation and teaching tools.
The platforms overlap and should not be assigned exclusively to individual uses. gsuite supports analysis, methods and software development. gsim supports method development and validation. gact supports data analysis and interpretation. qgteach connects research results with teaching.
The important point is cumulative. AI helped develop the infrastructure, and AI assistants can now use and extend what has already been built.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Using and extending the infrastructure


Use existing capabilities

Inspect the data and available tools
Specify the scientific model
Run and assess the analysis
Save the script and report


Add a missing capability

Identify the limitation
Define the required method or computation
Implement it using existing components
Validate and document the extension


Each completed project can improve the infrastructure available to the next.

From conversation to a reproducible analysis · From a scientific question to a supported model


AI assistants can work with the existing platforms rather than starting each project from scratch. They can inspect the available functionality, run analyses, modify code, add interfaces and prepare documentation.
Researchers remain responsible for defining the scientific problem, reviewing the statistical and computational decisions, and deciding whether the evidence is sufficient.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Data analysis infrastructure: gact
How can we make data from different sources usable in the same analysis?


Prepare and connect

Detect and validate data structures
Harmonise GWAS summary statistics
Add biological annotations
Record reusable ingestion steps


Analyse and interpret

Connect variants with genes and pathways
Use established statistical methods
Trace results back to their sources
Preserve the complete analysis workflow


The value comes from making data usable together.

gact


gact contains schema detection, normalisation and validation of GWAS summary statistics, ingestion recipes, biological annotation sets and database access. Existing tutorials connect these resources to gene analysis, fine-mapping and pathway analysis, including methods supplied by qgg.
This example concerns data preparation, connection and interpretation. It does not imply that every statistical method belongs within gact or that all four platforms already form one integrated pipeline.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Simulation for method development: gsim
How well does a method recover known quantities under different scenarios?


Define the scenario

Pedigree and population structure
Genetic architecture and effects
Phenotypes and environmental variation
Quantities that the method should recover


Assess the method

Compare estimates with known truth
Examine uncertainty and failures
Change the scenario and repeat
Identify where the method struggles


Simulation helps us develop, compare and refine methods under conditions where the truth is known.

gsim


gsim provides simulation infrastructure rather than owning every benchmark. It supports pedigrees, genotype and phenotype simulation, multiple genetic architectures and retained simulation truth. Study designs and evaluation metrics belong in the assessment workflow, for example sblrbench.
Our 10,000-animal pedigree examples use simulation to compare estimates and breeding values with known quantities. Replicated scenarios assess statistical behaviour. Independent small numerical references still provide a separate check of the implementation.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: Software from algorithms to interfaces: gsuite
text:
Software from algorithms to interfaces: gsuite







Layer
Examples




User interface
R functions such as gfit() and gvc()


Reusable model components
Covariance models, estimation and prediction


Native C++ and shared libraries
Solver interfaces, factor reuse and diagnostics


Numerical algorithms
Sparse solves and selected inverse entries



Development connects statistical ideas to efficient and usable software.

gsuite


Read the layers from bottom to top. Development includes numerical algorithms, native C++, shared libraries, reusable model components and the R interface. CHOLMOD and PARDISO are established external solvers that we build on. Our selected inverse uses retained CHOLMOD factors. The YAMS analogy concerns computing needed inverse entries, not a YAMS dependency.
greml owns model computations and gsolve owns solvers. The R interface exposes supported combinations. A Python interface remains a possible future addition and is therefore not presented here as a current capability.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
The libraries behind gsuite








Repository
Main responsibility




gsuite
R interface: models, computational tasks and results


greml
Mixed models, REML estimation and prediction


gsolve
Numerical solvers, factor reuse and selected inverse calculations


gmat
Matrix operations, genotype panels and linkage disequilibrium


gbits
Compact genotype storage and operations on packed data


gcorr
Genetic correlation calculations


gscore
Genetic scoring and prediction


gbayes
Bayesian regression models




gsolve connects our model computations to established numerical libraries:
CHOLMOD / SuiteSparse and PARDISO → sparse matrix factorisation and linear solves.

This is a responsibility map, not a complete dependency graph. gsuite exposes selected capabilities through its R interface. gsim is a separate R package for simulation.
CHOLMOD and PARDISO are external libraries, not software developed by us. gsolve provides interfaces that allow supported model computations to use these sparse numerical backends. Other dense and iterative routes also exist.
Our selected-inverse implementation builds on retained CHOLMOD supernodal factors. It calculates required inverse entries without forming the full dense inverse. It does not use PARDISO for selected inversion.
AI-assisted development includes the algorithms and infrastructure around these external libraries, their integration, and the statistical and R layers.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: Reusable computational building blocks in gsuite
text:
Reusable computational building blocks in gsuite





Model specification leads to sparse mixed-model equations, factorization and solves, reuse of numerical quantities, and a REML update. The update returns to assembly for the next iteration.



Reused quantities

MME solutions and quadratic forms
Log determinants from factorizations
Selected inverse entries for trace terms
Derivative solves and cross-products

REML calculations

Restricted log likelihood
Score: first derivatives
Information: second-order curvature
Average Information for parameter updates


Reuse the same building blocks for estimation, prediction and uncertainty.

Architecture · Numerical foundation


The model specification supplies the design matrices and covariance components. From these, we assemble the mixed-model coefficient matrix and right-hand side. In the standard notation, the coefficient matrix contains terms formed from X, Z, inverse residual covariance and inverse random-effect covariance.
The sparse factorization supports several calculations. We use it to solve the mixed-model equations and obtain quadratic forms. The factorization also provides the coefficient-matrix log determinant. The covariance components provide the other determinant terms required by the restricted likelihood.
Selected inverse entries provide the trace terms needed by the direct sparse route. Derivative solves and cross-products contribute to the score and information calculations.
The score contains the first derivatives of the restricted likelihood. Observed and expected information describe second-order curvature. The Average Information matrix provides an efficient curvature calculation for updating the covariance parameters.
After each update, we rebuild the parameter-dependent parts and repeat the calculation. At the final covariance estimates, the same solver infrastructure supports prediction and uncertainty calculations.
Within the ecosystem, gsuite provides the R-facing model specification, greml owns the mixed-model and REML calculations, and gsolve provides factorization and solver operations. This slide describes the sparse direct route. Other backends may use different numerical building blocks.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: Mathematical core of the same REML calculation
text:
Mathematical core of the same REML calculation


Mixed model
\[
y=X\beta+Zu+e,\qquad u\sim N(0,G),\quad e\sim N(0,R)
\]
Mixed-model equations
\[
C(\theta)
\begin{bmatrix}\widehat\beta\\\widehat u\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}X^\top R^{-1}y\\Z^\top R^{-1}y\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
C(\theta)=
\begin{bmatrix}
X^\top R^{-1}X & X^\top R^{-1}Z\\
Z^\top R^{-1}X & Z^\top R^{-1}Z+G^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Determinants for REML
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\log|V|+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|\\
&\qquad=\log|R|+\log|G|+\log|C|
\end{aligned}
\]

REML quantities
\[
\begin{aligned}
V &= ZGZ^\top+R\\
P &= V^{-1}-V^{-1}X(X^\top V^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top V^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
-2\ell_R(\theta) &= \mathrm{constant}+\log|V|\\
&\quad+\log|X^\top V^{-1}X|+y^\top Py
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(V_i=\partial V/\partial\theta_i\),
\[
s_i=\frac12\left[y^\top PV_iPy-\operatorname{tr}(PV_i)\right]
\]
\[
\mathcal I_O=-\frac{\partial^2\ell_R}{\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top}
\]
\[
\mathcal I_{AI,ij}=\frac12 y^\top PV_iPV_jPy
\]

Solves, selected inverse entries and derivative blocks supply these quantities.

Independent \(u,e\); positive-definite \(G,R\); full-rank \(X\). AI form shown for covariance components entering \(V\) linearly.
Architecture · Numerical foundation


The covariance parameters are collected in theta. They determine the residual covariance R, the random-effect covariance G, the marginal covariance V and the mixed-model coefficient matrix C.
The mixed-model equations provide estimates and predictions without forming the dense marginal covariance matrix V. The determinant identity expresses the two marginal REML determinant terms through R, G and the sparse mixed-model coefficient matrix C.
The restricted likelihood combines these determinant terms with the quadratic form y transpose P y.
For each parameter, V sub i is the derivative of V with respect to that parameter. The score is the first derivative of the restricted likelihood. It contains a quadratic term and a trace term.
The observed information is the negative second derivative of the likelihood. The Average Information matrix provides the curvature used for parameter updates. For variance components that enter V linearly, its familiar form is one half y transpose P V sub i P V sub j P y.
The implementation does not need to construct the dense P matrix. Sparse MME solves, selected inverse entries and derivative calculations provide the required quantities.
For nonlinear covariance parameterisations, transformation and chain-rule terms must also be included. The equations shown here describe the core variance-component formulation.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime
text:
gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime




Numerical agreement
50,000 animals
Maximum covariance-estimate difference below \(4.3\times10^{-8}\).
Prediction correlations essentially 1 on 1,000 preselected animals.
Competitive runtime on these three tested models.


gsuite 0.29.0 and DMU 5.6. Each bar represents one execution. The work boundaries differ: gsuite fitting versus DMU preprocessing and fitting.


Results, scope and provenance


The numerical results provide evidence for these frozen direct pedigree REML models. Covariance agreement covers the saved parameters. Prediction correlations exceed 0.999999999998 on the predeclared first 1,000 pedigree-coded animals, not all 50,000. Likelihood constants remain unreconciled. Timings are descriptive single runs with different work boundaries, so this is not a general speed claim or qualification of all current gsuite routes.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Teaching infrastructure: gteach
A common structure connects learning objectives with editable teaching material.


Source material

Learning objectives
R and Quarto source
Code, data and exercises
Speaker notes


Reusable outputs

Lecture slides
Worked tutorials
Interactive examples
Narrated presentations


We can develop the material together, then revise and reuse it across courses.

gteach


This is infrastructure for teaching, not only a collection of slides. The course scaffolding provides a consistent home for slides, notes, tutorials, exercises, apps and data. Narration tools use the speaker notes. Existing R and Shiny examples include genetic drift, selection and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
AI helps develop both the tools and the teaching content. We choose the learning objectives, review explanations and code, and check narration. The rename is planned; the current repository and links remain qgteach.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where will AI lead us?


What is likely to change

Writing, coding and analysis will become faster
More groups will develop advanced methods and software
AI assistants will perform increasingly complex tasks
Research roles and expectations will change


Questions for our programme

Which expertise and resources will distinguish us?
How should we combine AI with our data and infrastructure?
Which capabilities should we develop and share?
How should training, review and responsibility change?


What should we change now to remain scientifically distinctive as AI becomes part of research?

AI is already part of research, and its capabilities will continue to develop. Routine use of writing assistants or code generation will become common. The strategic question concerns how this changes our research and what will remain distinctive.
Scientific questions, domain knowledge, trusted data, critical evaluation and responsibility will remain important. Our shared platforms provide one possible advantage because they capture expertise in infrastructure that researchers and AI assistants can use and extend.
We should discuss which capabilities we need, how our roles may change, and where we should invest to remain scientifically strong.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: From a computational need to a component
text:
From a computational need to a component
Need: Obtain required inverse entries without forming a full dense inverse.







Step
What we work through with AI




Build small references
Dense inverse and scalar Takahashi calculations in C++


Implement the efficient algorithm
Selected inversion using retained CHOLMOD factors


Compare in native tests
Check requested entries against both references


Check computational behaviour
Factor reuse, thread agreement and retained solves


Integrate and assess
Supported model computations and the R workflow



Reference and production calculations are both native C++.

The development pattern is to establish a small reference, implement the efficient algorithm, compare them, and then check broader computational and user workflows. This describes the documented validation structure rather than asserting the exact historical order of every implementation step. gsolve/docs/testing.md and tests/test_supernodal_selected_inverse.cpp document and implement two small C++ references: a dense inverse and a separate scalar Takahashi recurrence. Requested entries from the production supernodal route are compared with both. The scalar reference is test-only, not an installed production fallback. Additional assertions check repeated factorisation, thread agreement, and preservation of retained solves and log-determinants. CHOLMOD is external; our production route uses its retained supernodal factors without forming the full dense inverse. PARDISO is not used for this selected inversion. These are test contracts, not a claim that every current test passes.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Different checks answer different questions







Check
Question it addresses




Mathematics and special cases
Does the formulation represent the intended model?


Small native reference versus production algorithm
Do separate computational approaches agree?


Repeated simulation with known truth
How well does the method recover quantities across scenarios?


Comparison with other software
Do results agree for matched models and settings?


Complete user workflow
Can the interface produce an interpretable, reproducible result?



Independence comes from a separate computational approach, not a different programming language.

These checks complement one another. Both reference and production code can be C++. greml retains small dense, analytical and finite-difference checks in native tests; gmat uses explicit dense correlation and LD calculations; gbits compares optimised implementations with scalar references. Their testing.md guides describe the assertions and reference limitations. Not every comparison has the same degree of independence: two wrappers over the same engine do not provide an independent numerical reference. Agreement between programs requires matching models, conventions and settings. Simulation can assess bias, uncertainty and prediction, but the generating model and studied scenarios limit what we learn. Runtime comparisons require explicit work boundaries. Define tolerances and acceptance criteria before interpreting results, and record the model, route and scale covered by the evidence.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where human judgement enters


Scientific decisions

Which question matters?
Which assumptions fit the study?
Which quantities should we estimate?
What can the results support?


Development decisions

Which approximations are acceptable?
What should be implemented or reused?
Which checks are sufficient?
When is a result ready to share?


AI can help examine each decision. We remain responsible for accepting it.

Human judgement is present throughout the process, not only in a final review. The researcher contributes study knowledge and statistical reasoning; software developers contribute computational and engineering judgement. AI can propose alternatives, expose assumptions, implement choices and assemble checks. Important decisions should remain visible in model definitions, code review, documentation and the interpretation of the evidence.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What remains after the conversation?


A reusable analysis or method

Model definition and assumptions
Code and an executable example
Tests and numerical evidence


Enough information to revisit it

Data identity, settings and versions
Results and documented limitations
Explanations and teaching material


The next researcher should be able to understand and use the work without reading the chat.

Conversation helps us develop the work, but it is not a substitute for its reproducible outputs. Keep the relevant data provenance, source revisions, settings and random seeds alongside results. Documentation should describe the final implementation and its limitations. Store reviewed evidence rather than every temporary experiment. This is what lets progress in one project benefit another, with or without the same assistant.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
text:
A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
The question: can existing building blocks support a family of methods for heritability and genetic correlation?







Analysis
Implemented method families




Genome-wide and annotation-based
LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer


Regional
HESS/rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA, LAVA


Conditional relationships
LAVA regression and partial genetic correlations



Native calculations in gcorr, reusable LD resources in gmat, numerical components in gsolve, and a common gsuite R interface.
The outcome includes working examples, diagnostics and documented limits.

Implemented capabilities


This is a concrete example of developing methods with an assistant. The starting point was existing software, including an LDSC core and sparse LD machinery. The question above is a summary of the initiating discussion, not a verbatim quote.
These are implementations of established method families, with bounded supported options. They are not claims of complete parity with every original package. The common interface preserves different meanings of annotation components, category totals and regional quantities, and method-specific uncertainty.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: How the researcher and assistant worked
text:
How the researcher and assistant worked








Step
Researcher
Assistant




Define the next capability
Set the scientific question and scope
Inspect equations and existing components


Implement and check
Review assumptions and challenge results
Write native code; compare small numerical oracles


Connect and evaluate
Decide what is supported and what needs investigation
Add the R interface, examples and simulations



Short, reviewed steps: specify → implement → test → discuss → commit.
The checks included independent calculations, selected upstream comparisons, R/native agreement and simulated data with known truth.

The conversation repeatedly narrowed scope: native libraries first, reuse existing components, keep the interface simple, and do not equate successful execution with statistical validity. The researcher chose the next milestone and reviewed the result before committing. The assistant investigated failures and updated code, tests and documentation.
Evidence was collected as the work progressed. For example, native uncertainty evaluations exposed undercoverage in some settings. Those limits were recorded, not removed by presenting only passing examples. Numerical oracles were small, independent reference calculations, distinct from the production algorithms.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
What is AI?







Term
Meaning




Artificial intelligence
The broad field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence


Machine learning and deep learning
Methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers


Generative AI
Models that generate text, code, images, audio or other content


AI assistants and agents
Systems built around generative AI that can work with users, files and tools. Agents can carry out multistep tasks



This presentation focuses on AI assistants and agents used for data analysis, method and software development, and teaching.

People use the term AI in different ways. Some think of machine learning or deep neural networks used to analyse data. Others think primarily of generative tools such as ChatGPT.
Machine learning covers methods that learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a form of machine learning based on neural networks with many layers. Modern generative AI is largely based on deep learning, but its purpose is to generate new content rather than only produce predictions.
Assistants interact with users and may have access to files and tools. Agents can use these capabilities to carry out more complex, multistep tasks.
This presentation concerns practical AI-assisted work. Applying machine learning as the scientific method being studied is outside its scope.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
How researchers use generative AI







Activity
Examples




Writing and communication
Draft, revise, translate and shorten text


Literature work
Find relevant papers, summarise them and compare their conclusions


Data analysis
Inspect data, write code, make figures and explain results


Teaching
Develop slides, exercises, examples and explanations


Administration
Prepare emails, meeting notes, plans and reports



Writing and literature review are common entry points. The same technology can also contribute directly to mathematical, analytical and software work.

Many researchers first encounter generative AI as a writing assistant. It can also help identify literature, organise information, write analysis code and develop teaching material.
These uses still require review. Literature searches must be checked against the original sources, and scientific claims must not be accepted simply because the generated text sounds convincing.
The following slides focus on applications in method and software development.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Areas of AI-assisted work








Area
Example output
Reusable result




Data analysis
An analysis script and report
A reproducible analysis workflow


Method development
A statistical model or algorithm
A clearly defined method with validation evidence


Software development
R and C++ code, interfaces and documentation
Tested and maintainable software components


Teaching
Slides, simulations and worked examples
Editable teaching materials



AI can help with mathematical reasoning, coding, analysis and documentation. Researchers set the scientific direction, review the decisions and determine what evidence is sufficient.

These activities are connected but distinct. A data-analysis question may reveal the need for a new statistical method. The method must then be translated into reliable software before it can be used routinely. A validated implementation can support new analyses and become a teaching example.
AI is particularly useful at the connection between mathematics and software. It can help examine equations, compare algorithms, implement them in R or C++, and prepare numerical checks. Researchers define the scientific problem, review the statistical and computational decisions, and decide what evidence is required.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Platforms developed with AI assistance







Platform
Purpose




gsuite
Statistical models, numerical computation and user interfaces


gsim
Simulation of genetic data and assessment of methods


gact
Data integration, annotation, analysis and interpretation


gteach
Shared tools and materials for teaching



AI has contributed to developing the platforms themselves. The resulting infrastructure can now support further work with AI assistants.

gtools


These platforms represent substantial outputs from AI-assisted development. The work has included mathematics, numerical algorithms, R and C++ code, interfaces, documentation, simulation, data organisation and teaching tools.
The platforms overlap and should not be assigned exclusively to individual uses. gsuite supports analysis, methods and software development. gsim supports method development and validation. gact supports data analysis and interpretation. qgteach connects research results with teaching.
The important point is cumulative. AI helped develop the infrastructure, and AI assistants can now use and extend what has already been built.

section: From numerical algorithms to an analysis package
text:
From numerical algorithms to an analysis package







Layer
Components in and around gsuite




Numerical computation
Sparse solves and the inverse entries needed for model calculations


Native C++ and shared libraries
Solver interfaces, reuse of calculations and diagnostics


Reusable model components
Covariance models, estimation, prediction and computational tasks


R interface
Model specification and results through gfit() and gvc()



The solver infrastructure uses established numerical libraries: CHOLMOD / SuiteSparse and PARDISO.

Architecture · Numerical foundation


Read the table from top to bottom, following the development from algorithms to the user interface. gsuite is the R-facing package; the numerical and statistical components live in focused libraries behind it.
CHOLMOD and PARDISO are external libraries. The gsolve selected-inverse implementation uses retained CHOLMOD factors. It computes needed inverse entries without forming the full dense inverse; PARDISO is not used for that selected-inverse route. The work also includes the surrounding solver infrastructure, reuse, model computations and R integration.
A Python interface remains a possible future addition, not a current claim. The technical deck contains the repository map and equations.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: From a scientific question to a model
text:
From a scientific question to a model


Each extension can add capabilities that other models can reuse.


From a scientific question to a supported model


The gsuite ecosystem is a collection of reusable computational building blocks. A scientific question determines the model and method, which determine the components required. Existing components may already provide what is needed. Otherwise, development adds the missing components to the collection.
Availability does not establish that a particular combination is supported. The assembled model still needs statistical and numerical validation, including reference calculations and checks of assumptions, convergence and predictions. AI can help identify, combine, implement and check components. Researchers and developers define the scientific meaning and decide what evidence is sufficient. Code that runs becomes a supported model only after its statistical meaning and numerical behaviour have been checked.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A shared collection of building blocks
text:
A shared collection of building blocks


Existing capabilities can be combined and extended to support new models and methods.


These are conceptual groups, not a repository dependency graph or a claim that every combination is currently supported. gsuite provides the R interface; related libraries provide reusable model and numerical components.
Bayesian and non-Bayesian methods can share data handling, model structures, matrix operations and solves. They also require different inference machinery. Bayesian building blocks already exist in sblr. The plan is to organise these capabilities into gbayes and integrate them with gsuite. This is primarily about making existing machinery reusable across the ecosystem, rather than developing Bayesian methods from scratch. Each new integration and model combination still requires appropriate checks.
Reusable components make focused extensions possible. The amount of new work depends on the model, and an extension may require substantial algorithmic work. The value is cumulative: checked components remain available for later methods.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Developing gsuite with AI


Mathematics and design

Discuss the model and its assumptions
Derive the required computations
Compare algorithms and special cases
Decide what to implement or reuse


Implementation and review

Work directly with the R and C++ code
Compile and run focused checks
Inspect failures and revise the approach
Retain reviewed code and documentation


AI assistance connects statistical ideas with their implementation.

ChatGPT supported discussion of statistical models, mathematics and software design. Codex supported work directly in the repositories. The assistant can examine the code, make a focused change, build it, run checks and explain the result.
This has made it possible to work through several layers in the same conversation. The developer remains the editor: defining the purpose, questioning assumptions, reviewing decisions and deciding what evidence is sufficient.
A concrete computational example was obtaining selected inverse entries from retained sparse factors. The task connects a mathematical requirement in REML with an algorithm, a native implementation and a reusable solver capability.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Checking the calculations







Check
Concrete example from the work




Small reference calculations
Compare the efficient selected inverse with dense and scalar references in C++


Computational behaviour
Check factor reuse, thread agreement and retained solves


Independent software comparison
Compare matched pedigree models with DMU on 50,000 animals


User workflow
Fit models through R and inspect summaries, predictions and diagnostics



In the saved DMU comparison, covariance estimates differed by less than \(4.3\times10^{-8}\).

Historical comparison: gsuite 0.29.0 and DMU 5.6; three frozen pedigree models. Results and scope


Both the small references and the efficient selected-inverse algorithm are native C++. The references include a dense inverse and a separate scalar Takahashi calculation. Independence comes from the different computational approaches, not from using different programming languages.
The saved DMU evidence covers single-trait, multitrait and longitudinal models. The numerical agreement is concrete evidence for those versions, models and settings. It does not qualify every current capability. The following slide shows historical runtime evidence. Individual desktop timings varied markedly in later reruns.
Checks must continue as the software changes. A recent current-version multitrait rerun reached estimates close to the historical endpoint but failed its line-search requirement. That remains a failure to investigate, not a successful current-version benchmark. Running code and supported models are not the same acceptance state.

section: gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime
text:
gsuite versus DMU: agreement and runtime




Numerical agreement
50,000 animals
Maximum covariance-estimate difference below \(4.3\times10^{-8}\).
Prediction correlations essentially 1 on 1,000 preselected animals.
Competitive runtime on these three tested models.


gsuite 0.29.0 and DMU 5.6. Each bar represents one execution. The work boundaries differ: gsuite fitting versus DMU preprocessing and fitting.


Results, scope and provenance


The numerical results provide evidence for these frozen direct pedigree REML models. Covariance agreement covers the saved parameters. Prediction correlations exceed 0.999999999998 on the predeclared first 1,000 pedigree-coded animals, not all 50,000. Likelihood constants remain unreconciled. Timings are descriptive single runs with different work boundaries, so this is not a general speed claim or qualification of all current gsuite routes.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A pedigree analysis as a conversation
text:
A pedigree analysis as a conversation
How much genetic variation is present in body weight, and how accurately can breeding values be predicted?


Work through the analysis

Check pedigree, observations and missing values
Discuss fixed effects and genetic effects
Fit the model and check convergence
Inspect estimates and predictions
Save the R script, figures and report


Keep the model explicit
fit <- gfit(
  formula = BW ~ sex + cohort + herd + (1 | id),
  data = data,
  pedigree = pedigree,
  task = "reml",
  control = fit_control
)
summary(fit)
Ordinary R data frames; a model that can be reviewed and rerun.


Analysis with an assistant · Worked example: 10,000 pedigree animals


This code follows the single-trait pedigree tutorial. The data frames and fit_control are prepared in that tutorial; the slide is an excerpt, not a standalone analysis script. The saved example has 10,000 pedigree animals, with 8,588 animals observed.
The assistant can help inspect identifiers, missingness and covariates, explain the model and run the code. Researchers review which effects belong in the analysis and what the resulting estimates mean. The report should include variance estimates, fit status and diagnostic plots, not just a fitted object.
Simulation truth supports the teaching example. Real data require scientific interpretation and sensitivity checks; a plausible plot does not establish that the model assumptions are correct.

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
section: A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
text:
A concrete case: GWAS summary statistics
The question: can existing building blocks support a family of methods for heritability and genetic correlation?







Analysis
Implemented method families




Genome-wide and annotation-based
LDSC, GNOVA, SumHer


Regional
HESS/rho-HESS, SUPERGNOVA, LAVA


Conditional relationships
LAVA regression and partial genetic correlations



Native calculations in gcorr, reusable LD resources in gmat, numerical components in gsolve, and a common gsuite R interface.
The outcome includes working examples, diagnostics and documented limits.

Implemented capabilities


This is a concrete example of developing methods with an assistant. The starting point was existing software, including an LDSC core and sparse LD machinery. The question above is a summary of the initiating discussion, not a verbatim quote.
These are implementations of established method families, with bounded supported options. They are not claims of complete parity with every original package. The common interface preserves different meanings of annotation components, category totals and regional quantities, and method-specific uncertainty.

Step
Researcher
Assistant

Write native code; compare small numerical oracles

title: AI-assisted research, methods, software and teaching
text:
Where is AI taking research?


What is likely to change

Writing, coding and analysis will become faster
More groups will develop advanced methods and software
AI assistants will perform increasingly complex tasks
Research roles and expectations will change


Questions for the programme

Which expertise and resources will distinguish the programme?
How can AI be combined with the available data and infrastructure?
Which capabilities should be developed and shared?
How should training, review and responsibility change?


What needs to change now for the programme to remain scientifically distinctive as AI becomes part of research?

AI is already part of research, and its capabilities will continue to develop. Routine use of writing assistants or code generation will become common. The strategic question concerns how this changes research and what will remain distinctive.
Scientific questions, domain knowledge, trusted data, critical evaluation and responsibility will remain important. Shared platforms provide one possible advantage because they capture expertise in infrastructure that researchers and AI assistants can use and extend.
Discussion can focus on the capabilities required, changing research roles, and investments that support scientific strength.
The gsuite experience suggests connecting applied research and development through manageable scientific questions. Each project can leave reusable analyses, checked components and documented evidence for later work. Scientific quality, review effort and maintenance matter alongside time saved.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
This example uses artificial data supplied with gsuite: 96 reference individuals, 48 markers in six regions and three continuous-trait summary datasets. It demonstrates the complete workflow on a tiny analysis universe, not a realistic genome-wide study or a test of statistical calibration. The method guide explains assumptions and the capability table lists support.
Run the blocks in order in a development installation of gsuite. They write only to build/examples/summary-statistic-workflow/, relative to the working directory. Running them again reuses the saved LD reference.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Read the supplied inputs
library(gsuite)
input <- system.file("extdata", "summary-statistic", package = "gsuite")
stopifnot(nzchar(input))
out <- file.path("build", "examples", "summary-statistic-workflow")
dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

observed <- read.delim(file.path(input, "statistics.tsv"))
categories <- read.delim(file.path(input, "annotation.tsv"))
annotation <- as.matrix(categories[c("baseline", "category")])
rownames(annotation) <- categories$marker
regions <- split(observed$marker, observed$region)
traits <- c("A", "B", "C")
stat <- setNames(lapply(traits, function(trait) {
  data.frame(marker = observed$marker, z = observed[[trait]],
             n = observed$n, block = observed$region)
}), traits)
All markers and alleles are already aligned. For real studies, alignment is a separate task. The six regions also serve as toy jackknife blocks; six blocks are too few for a well-supported genome-wide uncertainty analysis. Block design and LD-reference suitability need scientific justification in a real study.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Prepare LD once
saved <- file.path(out, "LDlist.rds")
source_files <- file.path(input, c("reference.bed", "reference.bim",
                                 "reference.fam", "annotation.tsv"))
source_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(source_files))
if (!file.exists(saved)) {
  # Work on copies; the installed example data are never removed.
  copies <- file.path(out, basename(source_files[1:3]))
  stopifnot(all(file.copy(source_files[1:3], copies, overwrite = TRUE)))
  Glist <- gs_gprep(bedfiles = copies[1])
  LD <- ldprep(Glist, reference = "toy-reference", task = "sparseld",
               out_prefix = file.path(out, "reference-LD"),
               max_distance_bp = 0, max_distance_variants = 8,
               r2 = 0, nthreads = 1, overwrite = TRUE)
  LD <- ldprep(LDlist = LD, task = "scores", annotation = annotation)
  for (region in names(regions)) {
    LD <- ldprep(LDlist = LD, task = "eigen", markers = regions[[region]],
                 region_name = region)
  }
  attr(LD, "example_source_md5") <- source_md5
  saveRDS(LD, saved)
  rm(Glist, LD)
  stopifnot(all(file.remove(copies)))
}

LD <- readRDS(saved)
validate_LDlist(LD)
stopifnot(identical(attr(LD, "example_source_md5"), source_md5))
stopifnot(identical(stat$A$marker, LD$resource$markers$marker_id))
reference_before <- tools::md5sum(unlist(LD$resource$paths))
The LD files must remain at their recorded paths. Genotype input files are no longer needed by the analysis. Full regional eigensystems are saved once; methods verify and reuse them, applying their own component-selection rules. Here all within-region correlations are retained. Chromosome-local construction excludes between-region LD; this is an explicit assumption of this toy example. If example inputs change, use a new output directory rather than reusing an old reference. The input fingerprint guards against accidental stale reuse.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Genome-wide h2 and genetic correlation
# The simulation has no marginal inflation and independent sampling errors.
genome_h2 <- gcorr(stat, LD, method = "ldsc", task = "h2",
                   control = list(intercept = "fixed_one"))
genome_rg <- gcorr(stat, LD, method = "ldsc", task = "rg",
                   control = list(intercept = "fixed_one", overlap_intercept = 0))
summary(genome_h2)
summary(genome_rg)
genome_rg$matrices[[LD$reference]]$reference$all$rg
plot(genome_rg)
“Genome-wide” here means the complete 48-marker analysis universe. Fixed intercepts are justified by the data generator, not recommended as universal defaults. gcorr() otherwise estimates LDSC intercepts. Check estimates, uncertainty and diagnostics together; a point estimate alone is not evidence of a nonzero genetic correlation.
For the bundled data, the genome-wide h2 estimates are approximately:



Trait

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Partition by annotation
partitioned <- gcorr(stat, LD, annotation = annotation,
                     method = "ldsc", task = "h2",
                     control = list(intercept = "fixed_one"))
partitioned$estimates
plot(partitioned, scope = "annotation_category")
partitioned$details[partitioned$details$quantity == "tau", ]

# The same columns can instead define SumHer architecture components.
architecture <- gcorr(stat, LD, annotation = annotation,
                      method = "sumher", task = "rg",
                      control = list(tagging = ld_scores(LD), overlap_intercept = 0))
architecture$matrices[[LD$reference]]$architecture_component
The subset overlaps the baseline, so category heritabilities must not be added together. In SumHer the columns define model components, a different estimand. Ordinary LD scores are an explicit illustrative choice of tagging weights; tagging and model-weighted scores are separate inputs. Differences between LDSC and SumHer on these data do not identify which estimator is preferable.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Regional analysis
# Region methods do not use score-method jackknife labels.
regional_stat <- lapply(stat, function(s) s[c("marker", "z", "n")])
sampling <- diag(length(traits))
dimnames(sampling) <- list(traits, traits)
regional_control <- list(sampling_correlation = sampling,
                         explained_ld_fraction = 1)
regional <- gcorr(regional_stat, LD, regions = regions,
                  method = "lava", task = "rg", control = regional_control)
summary(regional)
regional$matrices[[LD$reference]]$region$region1$cov
plot(regional)
All traits share one fit per region. The identity sampling-correlation matrix matches the independent noise columns in the generator. It must be replaced by an appropriate overlap model for real data. This call provides point estimates and univariate screening; it does not request bivariate simulation inference. An rg plot without bars therefore does not imply exact estimation.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
Conditional relationships
conditional_control <- regional_control
conditional_control$inference <- list(seed = 42, pvalue_draws = 2000,
                                      interval_draws = 2000)
partial <- gcorr(regional_stat, LD, regions = regions,
                 method = "lava", task = "partial_rg",
                 targets = c("A", "B"), conditioned_on = "C",
                 control = conditional_control)
regression <- gcorr(regional_stat, LD, regions = regions,
                    method = "lava", task = "regression",
                    outcome = "A", predictors = c("B", "C"),
                    control = conditional_control)
summary(partial)
plot(partial)
regression$estimates
regression$details[regression$details$quantity %in%
                    c("r_squared", "explained_genetic_variance"), ]
vapply(partial$diagnostics, function(d) d$inference$pvalue_precision_met,
       logical(1))
Partial rg asks about the A/B genetic relationship conditional on C. Regression predicts the regional genetic component of A from B and C. Neither establishes causality. Inference checks native eligibility and conditioning requirements; unavailable results remain missing with reasons.
The small simulation budgets keep this example quick. Inspect Monte Carlo precision, retained draws and budget flags before interpreting p-values or intervals. A very small reported p-value can still have inadequate Monte Carlo precision. These intervals have no simultaneous coverage or automatic multiple-testing correction.



Partial genetic correlation between A and B conditional on C in the six artificial regions. Bars are native 95% simulation intervals for the fixed seed and 2,000-draw example.


In this run, the p-value precision target is met for regions 4 and 5, but not for regions 1, 2, 3 and 6. A small p-value does not remove the need to inspect its Monte Carlo diagnostics. The figure illustrates the workflow rather than establishing significance, calibration or a causal relationship.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
section: Save the analysis and verify reuse
text:
Save the analysis and verify reuse
fits <- list(genome_h2 = genome_h2, genome_rg = genome_rg,
             partitioned = partitioned, architecture = architecture,
             regional = regional, partial = partial, regression = regression)
saveRDS(fits, file.path(out, "fits.rds"))
results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(name) {
  cbind(analysis = name, fits[[name]]$estimates)
}))
write.csv(results, file.path(out, "estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(reference_before, tools::md5sum(unlist(LD$resource$paths))))
stopifnot(all(vapply(regional$diagnostics, function(d) d$eigensystem_reused,
                    logical(1))))
Keep the fits, input provenance and diagnostics with the report. Re-running the blocks in a fresh R session reads the saved LDlist and leaves its files unchanged. This verifies resource reuse, not the suitability of the reference for another population or the correctness of an unverified alignment.

title: From a saved LD reference to genetic analysis
text:
What has been checked
The exact tutorial blocks ran successfully in separate R processes, with identical result tables and unchanged saved LD files. The focused gcorr/LDlist suite passed 587 checks, including direct R-to-native comparisons, saved spectra, binary/mixed inputs in the method tests and explicit unavailable-result handling. The illustrated tutorial itself uses continuous traits.
These checks validate the implementation and workflow. They do not establish calibration on realistic GWAS data, upstream-software parity, a clean package-wide release qualification or support on untested platforms.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
gbayes() exposes the native Bayesian regression library through gsuite. Use gmap() for regional fine-mapping and colocalisation; use gbayes() when the main result is a regression fit, parameter learning and marker effects. Both interfaces reuse the same native samplers.
For one continuous trait, stat is a data frame with marker, allele1, allele2, beta_std and n, in exactly the marker and allele order of an LDlist prepared by ldprep(). allele1 is the counted allele. Alignment is a separate task: no markers are flipped or removed here.
beta_std means the marginal effect on a standardized phenotype per standardized dosage. A raw per-allele GWAS beta must be converted using compatible genotype and phenotype scales before it is passed here. Do not rename a raw beta or z-score column to beta_std. The native preparation uses
\[
C = D_N^{1/2} R D_N^{1/2}, \qquad s_j = N_j\widehat\beta_{j,\mathrm{std}}.
\]
Here \(R\) is the supplied LD correlation matrix. With common sample size \(N\), \(C=NR\). Different sample sizes require explicit control=list(sample_size="variable"); this is an approximate Gaussian summary likelihood, not reconstruction of an unknown sample-overlap matrix.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
gbayes() exposes the native Bayesian regression library through gsuite. Use gmap() for regional fine-mapping and colocalisation; use gbayes() when the main result is a regression fit, parameter learning and marker effects. Both interfaces reuse the same native samplers.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
Fit and inspect
Specify variances on this standardized scale. They remain fixed unless learning is requested; the values below illustrate a choice, not a universal default.
library(gsuite)
fit <- gbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesr", trait="height",
  prior=list(residual_variance=1, effect_variance=.04,
             weights=c(.9,.04,.04,.02)),
  control=list(burnin=1000, sampling_sweeps=4000,
               seeds=c(31,97), threads=1))
fit
summary(fit)
head(fit$estimates)
fit$parameter_mean
fit$posterior
BayesR uses a null component and effect-variance multipliers c(0,.01,.1,1) by default. BayesC instead uses a single nonzero component and an inclusion_probability. The returned marker means, variances and PIPs pool the retained draws across chains. They are labelled by marker and alleles. These marginal PIPs are not component credible sets.
fit$posterior reports native parameter means, intervals, HPD intervals, R-hat, bulk effective sample sizes and Monte Carlo standard errors, with availability and estimation status. Fixed quantities are labelled as fixed; they do not provide evidence of convergence. fit$chains retains each chain’s marker means/PIPs and compact parameter traces. Marker draws are not retained. retain_diagnostics=FALSE disables these traces and reports their summaries as unavailable. Review diagnostics and sensitivity to prior choices before interpreting results; completing the requested sweeps does not certify convergence.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
section: Learn effect variance and mixture weights
text:
Learn effect variance and mixture weights
learned <- gbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesc", trait="height",
  prior=list(residual_variance=1, effect_variance=.04,
    inclusion_probability=.05,
    effect_variance_prior=list(df=4, scale=.04),
    weight_prior=c(38,2)),
  control=list(burnin=1000, sampling_sweeps=4000, seeds=c(31,97),
    estimate_effect_variance=TRUE, estimate_weights=TRUE))
summary(learned)
The variance hyperprior is scaled inverse chi-square; scale is not its mean. The weight hyperprior contains positive Dirichlet concentrations, null component first. The supplied effect variance and weights initialize learning. All updates and posterior summaries run in native gbayes. Residual variance remains fixed: its learning needs additional sufficient statistics and is not exposed here.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
section: A complete example and reusable effects
text:
A complete example and reusable effects
Download the R example. It uses gsim to simulate one trait for 10,000 individuals and 40 markers, prepares a full LD reference, fits fixed-parameter BayesR and learning BayesC, then applies posterior-mean effects to another dosage matrix. It also simulates three traits in the same individuals and fits a joint BayesR model with covariance and mixture-weight learning, as described below. Run it using development installations of gsuite and gsim:
source("run_gbayes_workflow.R")
result <- readRDS("build/examples/gbayes-workflow/workflow.rds")
summary(result$learned)
result$weights
result$scores
summary(result$multivariate$fit)
result$multivariate$fit$estimates$pip
result$multivariate$scores
Outputs stay under build/examples/gbayes-workflow; rerunning replaces those example outputs. Set options(gsuite.bayes.out="another-directory") first to choose a different location. The serializable result bundle contains both fits, statistics, LD descriptor, labelled weights and the coding needed for scoring. Fits can be inspected after reloading without reopening LD or genotype files.
Apply effects to dosage columns in the same order, with matching counted alleles and the same centering/scaling used in preparation:
weights <- fit$estimates[,c("marker","allele1","allele2","mean")]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(target), weights$marker))
target_z <- sweep(sweep(target, 2, center), 2, scale_x, "/")
score <- drop(target_z %*% weights$mean)
These scores have standardized phenotype units and no intercept. The calculation illustrates weight reuse, not prediction accuracy. Production scoring belongs in gscore; this milestone does not add a gscore R interface.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
Execution and current scope
The fit consumes existing sparse LD files and does not need genotype files. Default storage="memory" materializes sparse LD, including its reverse index, but never a dense matrix. max_ld_entries=1e7 limits stored upper-triangle entries; it is not a total RAM limit. Memory also grows with markers and chains. For larger resources, storage="disk" uses the native bounded column reader and requires threads=1. threads>1 with memory storage parallelizes chains, not marker updates. Exact seeds are recorded and thread allocation does not change a chain’s random-number stream.
Omitted LD entries are treated as zero. The supplied matrix is assumed positive semidefinite; truncating or thresholding LD can violate this, and the interface does not silently repair it. Reference mismatch remains a separate concern. The example uses complete, matching LD to keep these issues out of the demonstration.
Annotation controls and multiple reference panels/providers per trait remain native-only. Regional sets and colocalisation remain in the mapping workflow.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
Fit several traits jointly
Pass a uniquely named list of standardized summary-statistic data frames. Every trait must match the same complete LD marker/allele order. The return values use these trait names and marker IDs throughout; nothing is silently reordered.
stats3 <- list(height=height_stat, weight=weight_stat, lipid=lipid_stat)
traits <- names(stats3)
V <- matrix(.01,3,3); diag(V) <- .04
dimnames(V) <- list(traits,traits)

# Omega is a justified fixed sampling-error covariance, in the same trait order.
joint <- gbayes(stats3, LD, method="bayesr",
  prior=list(effect_covariance=V,
    pattern_weights=c(.9,rep(.1/7,7)),
    covariance_prior=list(df=6,scale=V*2),
    pattern_prior=c(18,rep(2/7,7)), component_prior=c(1,1,1)),
  sampling=list(dependence="shared_ld", covariance=Omega),
  control=list(burnin=1000, sampling_sweeps=2000, seeds=c(31,97),
    estimate_covariance=TRUE, estimate_pattern_weights=TRUE,
    estimate_component_weights=TRUE))

joint
summary(joint)
joint$estimates$mean                 # marker x trait posterior means
joint$estimates$pip                  # marker x trait marginal PIPs
joint$estimates$any_pip              # active in at least one trait
joint$parameter_mean$effect_covariance
joint$expected_trait_sharing        # expected marker counts per trait pair
joint$posterior                     # native intervals and chain diagnostics
effect_covariance is the covariance of latent base effects. It is not realised genetic covariance or genetic correlation: activity patterns, magnitude scales and LD also determine those quantities. The inverse-Wishart prior uses explicit degrees of freedom and a scale matrix. A proper prior requires \(\nu>T-1\); its mean is \(\Psi/(\nu-T-1)\) when \(\nu>T+1\). Learning is optional and all three flags default to FALSE; omit unused hyperpriors for fixed-parameter fits.

State the sampling assumptions







Input
Meaning and requirements




sampling=list(dependence="independent", residual_variance=c(height=1,weight=1,lipid=1))
Explicitly independent sampling errors. Common sample sizes may differ between traits. Genetic effects can still be correlated.


sampling=list(dependence="shared_ld", covariance=Omega)
Correlated sampling errors with common N across all traits/markers, one shared LD operator and a fixed positive-definite covariance.



Shared LD uses \(E(S)=CB\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}S)=\Omega\otimes C\). Omega is neither a genetic covariance matrix nor a matrix of overlap counts. The simulated example obtains it from the known residual covariance, transformed to standardized phenotype units. Real data need a justified estimate/input on that scale. The interface does not infer overlap or estimate this covariance. Arbitrary differing LD and marker-specific overlap are outside this route.
Independent summaries additionally allow control=list(sample_size="variable"). That approximation requires explicit named sampling$study_sample_size metadata as well as per-marker n. Study sizes do not replace the per-marker values. No mean or maximum sample size is invented. Residual scales stay fixed in both modes.


Activity patterns and magnitude components
With three traits, the native default pattern order is 000,100,010,110,001,101,011,111: the first trait varies fastest and the null pattern comes first. pattern_weights assign probabilities to these patterns; the default is uniform. The example puts 0.9 on the null and shares 0.1 across the nonnull patterns.
Multivariate BayesC has one positive magnitude scale, 1. BayesR defaults to scales c(.01,.1,1) with equal weights conditional on a nonnull pattern. Unlike the single-trait weights argument, component_weights has no null component: null is already represented by pattern 000. This is a factorized pattern-by-scale mixture, not an unrestricted weight for every pattern/component combination. For BayesC, omit component_prior and estimate_component_weights.
Complete patterns are available for 2–12 traits, but there are \(2^T\) of them. For more traits, or a scientifically restricted model, supply an explicit binary matrix with labelled trait columns, unique row labels and the null first:
patterns <- rbind(none=rep(0,length(traits)), shared=rep(1,length(traits)))
colnames(patterns) <- traits
# Use prior=list(effect_covariance=V, patterns=patterns,
#                pattern_weights=c(none=.9,shared=.1)) for a fixed prior.
This changes the model to allow only those patterns; it is not an approximation to fitting every pattern. Every trait must appear in an allowed nonnull pattern. Trait count is not restricted to two or three. The native memory estimate is bounded by control$memory_limit_bytes (256 MiB by default), separately from LD storage and R result storage. Compact traces contain covariance and mixture parameters; all-marker draws and per-marker pattern-probability arrays are not retained.
The returned fit is serializable. To reuse the joint effects, multiply a compatible standardized dosage matrix by joint$estimates$mean; columns of the resulting score matrix retain the trait names. This demonstrates reuse and is not a prediction-accuracy assessment.

title: Bayesian regression from summary statistics
text:
Let annotations inform the prior
annotation separates three questions: which markers are active, which magnitude component they belong to, and their relative effect variance. It connects the existing native annotation models; it does not change the LD preparation or sampling-error assumptions.








Role
Single trait
Multiple traits




inclusion
BayesC logistic inclusion probability
Use pattern


pattern
Not applicable
Continuation-probit probabilities over declared trait patterns


component
BayesR continuation-probit probabilities, including the null component
BayesR probabilities over positive magnitudes, conditional on a nonnull pattern


variance
Centred log-linear relative effect variance
One marker multiplier scaling the latent effect-covariance matrix



Each role accepts its own numeric design matrix. Row names must match the LD marker IDs exactly; column names must be unique. Binary or continuous columns are allowed, including overlapping annotations. Native preparation centres each column across the supplied markers, without standardising it. Do not add an intercept column. Annotation units therefore affect the coefficient prior.
Using the data from the example script:
# Artificial annotations; they do not represent biological categories.
A <- cbind(category=as.numeric(seq_len(m) %% 3L==0), position=seq_len(m)/m)
rownames(A) <- ids

annotated <- gbayes(stat, LD, method="bayesc",
  prior=list(residual_variance=1/scale_y^2, effect_variance=.04,
             inclusion_probability=.05),
  annotation=list(inclusion=list(design=A), variance=list(design=A)),
  control=ctl)

annotated_joint <- gbayes(stats3, LD, method="bayesr",
  prior=list(effect_covariance=V, pattern_weights=pattern_weights),
  sampling=list(dependence="shared_ld", covariance=Omega),
  annotation=list(pattern=list(design=A), component=list(design=A),
                  variance=list(design=A)),
  control=list(burnin=1000, sampling_sweeps=2000, seeds=c(31,97)))

annotated$annotations$inclusion$coefficient_mean
annotated_joint$annotations$pattern$prior_probability_mean
annotated_joint$annotations$variance$multiplier_mean
annotated_joint$posterior  # coefficients, intervals and native chain diagnostics
These additional fits reuse the same 10,000 individuals and 40 markers. They illustrate model specification and returned quantities, not evidence for annotation enrichment or a performance comparison.

Fixed coefficients, learning and interpretation
Each annotation model defaults to learn=TRUE, coefficient_prior_sd=1 and update_every=1. Set learn=FALSE to hold its coefficients fixed. For inclusion or variance models, initial is a vector named in design-column order; omitted values start at zero. For example:
annotation=list(variance=list(design=A, learn=FALSE,
                             initial=c(category=.2, position=-.1)))
BayesC inclusion uses a logistic model around inclusion_probability, which remains the baseline at zero centred annotations. It may still be learned with estimate_weights=TRUE and weight_prior. Its coefficient update uses a fixed random-walk proposal_sd=.1; proposal and acceptance counts are returned per chain. There is no automatic proposal adaptation.
Pattern/component annotations instead replace global weight learning for that axis. Disable estimate_weights for scalar BayesR, or the corresponding estimate_pattern_weights / estimate_component_weights flag for multivariate fits. Global weights still supply default intercept-prior centres. Other axes and effect-variance/covariance learning can remain enabled.
Continuation-probit models follow the declared category order. Each stick is labelled by the category where it can stop; the last category has no stick. Scalar BayesR labels are component_0,... (null first); multivariate magnitude labels are component_1,... (positive scales only). Pattern labels are the rows of prior$patterns. Optional intercept_means is named in stick order. Optional initial is a matrix with rows (Intercept) followed by annotation names, and columns in stick order. intercept_prior_sd defaults to 1. Changing category order changes this prior model.
Variance annotations multiply the base variance/covariance by \(\exp(\widetilde A_j\theta)\). At each draw these multipliers have geometric mean one across markers; their posterior means need not. There is no variance intercept. The native elliptical-slice update uses maximum_evaluations=10000 by default; exhausted budgets raise an error.
fit$annotations contains coefficient means/variances, design means, labelled marker prior probabilities or variance multipliers, and per-chain coefficient traces and update counts. Prior probabilities are averaged over retained draws; they are not posterior marker PIPs, which remain in fit$estimates. Coefficient intervals and diagnostics join fit$posterior. Fixed coefficients are labelled as fixed; retain_diagnostics=FALSE disables traces and intervals while retaining posterior means. Review mixing before interpreting coefficients, especially for correlated or weakly informed annotations. Annotation-group covariance models and partitioned genetic-variance summaries are not exposed here.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Prepare instruments from aligned GWAS summaries and an existing LDlist, then fit a method to that saved preparation. All selection, LD filtering, HEIDI and estimation calculations use native gcorr components. Alignment is a separate task.
Download the complete example. It constructs 12 candidate variants with exactly independent LD and outcome effects close to 0.3 times exposure effects. This is a workflow illustration, not a simulation study or a comparison of statistical accuracy. It writes one result bundle, estimate table, figure and reference files under build/examples/mr-workflow. The reference has 1,024 artificial individuals; the illustrative GWAS sample-size metadata are 100,000 and 90,000. No individual-level GWAS is simulated.
library(gsuite)
source("run_mr_workflow.R")
example <- readRDS("build/examples/mr-workflow/workflow.rds")
stat <- example$stat
LD <- example$LD
head(stat$X)
Each trait table contains marker, allele1, allele2, beta, se and n. allele1 is the counted allele. Both tables must match the same subset of the reference in its existing order, including alleles. Rows are not reordered or flipped. Sample sizes are provenance; GSMR does not use them as weights.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Prepare instruments from aligned GWAS summaries and an existing LDlist, then fit a method to that saved preparation. All selection, LD filtering, HEIDI and estimation calculations use native gcorr components. Alignment is a separate task.
Download the complete example. It constructs 12 candidate variants with exactly independent LD and outcome effects close to 0.3 times exposure effects. This is a workflow illustration, not a simulation study or a comparison of statistical accuracy. It writes one result bundle, estimate table, figure and reference files under build/examples/mr-workflow. The reference has 1,024 artificial individuals; the illustrative GWAS sample-size metadata are 100,000 and 90,000. No individual-level GWAS is simulated.
library(gsuite)
source("run_mr_workflow.R")
example <- readRDS("build/examples/mr-workflow/workflow.rds")
stat <- example$stat
LD <- example$LD
head(stat$X)
Each trait table contains marker, allele1, allele2, beta, se and n. allele1 is the counted allele. Both tables must match the same subset of the reference in its existing order, including alleles. Rows are not reordered or flipped. Sample sizes are provenance; GSMR does not use them as weights.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Prepare and inspect instruments
prepared <- gcorr(stat, LD, method = "gsmr", task = "prepare_mr",
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y",
  control = list(non_overlapping_samples = TRUE,
                 effect_units = c(X = "X units", Y = "Y units"),
                 ancestry = c(X = "artificial", Y = "artificial")))
print(prepared)
prepared$decisions
prepared$ld_decisions
Default preparation excludes missing estimates, very small standard errors and exposure associations above \(p=5\times10^{-8}\). It applies the original GSMR LD-pruning rule at \(r^2=0.1\), then filters retained correlations using reference sample size and BH-adjusted LD tests. At least ten instruments must remain. Use method="gsmr2" during preparation for its \(r^2=0.05\) default.
Pruning is degree-based, not significance-ranked clumping; input-order ties can change selection. Every candidate decision and every retained LD-pair decision is recorded. The prepared result is an ordinary serializable R list containing its selected statistics, filtered LD, metadata and decisions. It is not another LD reference format. saveRDS()/readRDS() preserves it without native pointers.
The initial interface materializes at most 2,048 candidate markers by default. Supply a bounded candidate set, not an entire GWAS. Omissions in a sparse reference remain zeros as stored; they do not prove population independence. An invalid or poorly conditioned filtered matrix returns an unavailable result rather than being silently repaired. Inspect available and reason.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Fit and examine results
gsmr <- gcorr(prepared, method = "gsmr", task = "mr")
gsmr2 <- gcorr(prepared, method = "gsmr2", task = "mr")
ivw <- gcorr(prepared, method = "ivw", task = "mr")
egger <- gcorr(prepared, method = "egger", task = "mr")
median <- gcorr(prepared, method = "weighted_median", task = "mr",
  control = list(seed = 19, bootstrap_replicates = 1000))
summary(gsmr)
gsmr$details$heidi
gsmr2$details$heidi$rounds
gsmr2$details$retained_original_indices
plot(gsmr)
These calls deliberately share the same prepared set. GSMR applies original HEIDI filtering; GSMR2 applies iterative global HEIDI. apply_heidi=FALSE disables that additional filtering. Preparation is never repeated during fitting. HEIDI indices refer to prepared rows; retained_original_indices maps the final subset back to the original candidate rows. All indices exposed in R are one-based.
IVW, Egger and weighted median use the preparation before HEIDI, and require approximately uncorrelated instruments. Their default absolute LD tolerance is \(10^{-8}\). Raising this tolerance does not add correlated-instrument uncertainty. The constructed example has exactly zero off-diagonal LD, so all five routes can use it. The weighted-median seed is explicit; generated draws are reproducible within the same C++ runtime, not necessarily across different toolchains.
Results label the exposure, outcome, method, estimate, SE and p-value. Egger also returns its intercept. Method-specific diagnostics include heterogeneity, exposure-strength measures, GSMR weights and ratio covariance, filtering results and bootstrap completion. Missing estimates mean unavailable, not zero effects. MR effects have outcome units per exposure unit; they are not genetic correlations.

title: Mendelian randomisation with prepared instruments
text:
Direction and interpretation
For reverse-direction MR, prepare again from the original candidate tables with exposure and outcome swapped. The reverse direction must select its own instruments; do not simply reverse a forward-selected set.
This interface supports univariable, non-overlapping-sample analyses with one matching reference ancestry. It does not infer sample overlap, correct for it, perform multivariable MR or convert binary-trait effects to liability scale. User-supplied effects retain their stated units.
Instrument association, a high F statistic, HEIDI filtering or colocalisation does not establish the exclusion restriction. IVW, Egger and weighted median rely on different assumptions about invalid instruments and pleiotropy. Treat their agreement as a diagnostic, not proof of causality. See also the colocalisation workflow.
